CURRIE (North Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 131) respecting pure foods.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Explain.

Pure food is now attracting world wide attention especially in respect to the conditions under which food is prepared for human consumption. The United States, the Australasian colonies, Great Britain herself, all civilized countries are. legislating in the direction of securing the purity of food. In Canada we have the Adulteration of Food Act, and we have the Canned Goods Act, and we have the Inspection of Foods Act, all directed more or less towafds this object, but to any one who has studied the subject it would appear that something is still wanting. This Bill among other things proposes to provide legislation for the establishing of standards of pure food, and in drafting the Bill I have endeavoured not to intrude upon the prerogatives of government by placing any charge upon the public or interfering with any trade. I trust the Minister of Inland Revenue, under whose jurisdiction

such matters come, will give this Bill careful consideration. My only regret is that some medical man who may understand the matter better than I, is not in charge of the Bill. This Bill provides that it shall be called the 'Pure Food Act', and that it shall be read and construed with the Adulteration Act, the Canned Goods Act, and the Inspection and Sales Act, and, following the precedents set by the legislature of Victoria it to some extent consolidates these Acts relating to pure food, and provides a uniform law on the subject. Under the heading of 'interpretation', the chief point is the definition of the words 'article of food' and for the purpose of this Bill an article of food is defined to be every article used for food or drink by man. Then, the Bill provides, similar to existing legislation, that an officer may enter upon and examine premises, and 'an officer' for the purpose of this Act is interpreted to be an officer under the meaning of the other Acts to which I have referred. The provisions with respect to seizure and so forth are similar to those in the Inspection and Sales Act and the Adulteration Act. This provision is made because there may be included in the standards fixed under this Bill certain things which are not contained in our present legislation.
Another clause provides that food put up for sale must bear a legible stamp or stencil mark, giving the name of the article, the quantity, measure, volume and so forth, and the name and address of the vendor or maker. The package must have on it, placed in a prominent position, in prominent letters, the words ' prepared under the regulations and standard of the Canadian Pure Foods Act.' The purpose is to give in a larger measure_ a guarantee to the public that these articles are properly prepared.
I find that other countries compel manufacturers to place a guarantee of this kind on their exported goods, so that it gives to the foreign consumer a certain guarantee of their quality. I desire that we should have the same law here, so that any foods or other articles of food that we sell abroad will carry with them a stamp of a pure food law of our own, such as is carried under the laws of the United States and Australia. The next subject that is dealt with is how samples should be taken in packages. Another clause concerning witnesses, provides that a witness need not be compelled to disclose where he obtains his information, also making a provision where and how an officer may purchase samples. Then another clause provides that the prosecution must be instituted within forty-two days after the information has been given, that is to limit the prosecution to a certain specified time. Then again when a person is summoned under this Act the summons is not 89
returnable for fourteen days. The next clause perhaps is one of the most important and defines what is meant by adulteration.
For the purposes of the Pure Food Act an article of food or substance or compound or other article shall be deemed adulterated or falsely described,
(a)	When it contains or is mixed with or diluted with any substance in any quality to the prejudice of the purchaser or consumer, or in any proportion which diminishes in any manner its food value or nutritive properties as compared with such article in a pure or normal state and in an undeteriorated or sound condition,
(b)	When it contains or is mixed with or diluted with any substance of lower commercial value than such article in pure or normal state and in an undeteriorated or sound condition, or
(c)	When it does not comply either wholly or in part with the standard therefor prescribed under this Act by any regulation, or
(d) When it contains any substance prescribed as a prohibited addition, or
(e) When it contains any substance concerning which any restrictive regulation has been made in excess of any quantity or proportion permitted by any such regulation, or
(f)	When it contains methyl alcohol, or not having paid customs or excise duty, it contains more than two parts of proof spirit per centum, or
(g)	When any article of food or other article or substance or compound in any package is described by any stamp or stencilled or impressed or printed or written statement or claim or brand or covering or label or mark or tag purporting to name or indicate the nature or quality or strength or purity or composition or origin or age or proportion of any article of food or ingredients or substances contained therein, which statement, claim, brand, covering label, mark or tag, is false or incorrect or misleading.
This clause in the Act virtually follows the Australian and American law. The next clause takes up the question of the addition of certain injurious drugs to liquors and wines, and provides that certain dangerous ingredients shall not be contained in them, such as cholorides, sulphites, sulphuric acid and other substances of that nature. The next clause deals with the quality of the tin which is supposed to be used in putting up a package, and makes provision against there being a dangerous quantity of lead in the covering or package. The next clause deals with toys, wall paper and articles of that kind, and provides that there shall be no arsenic in the paint used on them. Then another clause deals with the matter of use of dangerous compounds in wall paper, leathers, and so forth. This provision against the use, for instance, of arsenic and lead, is contained in the statute-books of other countries, and is borrowed largely from them. The principal clause deals with the question of who shall



fix these standards, and that is perhaps the most important section in this Act. It reads thus:
The Governor in Council may appoint for the purposes of this Act a pure foods standard commission.
(a)	Such commission shall be composed of fifteen members. The chief analyst of the Dominion shall be a member and shall preside as chairman of the commission. _
(b)	The other members of the commission must hold the position for the time being or have held the position of professor or teacher of any one of tlie following subjects in a recognized university in the Dominion of Canada, chemistry, biology, materia medica, physiology, agriculture, sanitation, bacteriology, veterinary science. The said members shall be appointed from the following faculties : One from a university in Nova Scotia, one from a university in jPrince Edward Island, one from a university in New Brunswick, one from the University of Laval, one from the University of McGill, one from the University of Queens, one from the University of Toronto, one from the Western University of London, one from a university in Manitoba, one from a university in Saskatchewan, one from a university in Alberta, one from a university in British Columbia, and two provincial medical health officers.
The commission shall have power to fix a standard for foods and drugs, and to establish regulations. In the United States this commission is composed of three officers of the government who frame regulations and fix the standard. There has been considerable difiiculty and controversy over these standards, and in order to avoid any theories or fads in the establishment of our standards, I think it would be wise for us to have a board of experts as large as possible, and composed of men who would be above reproach in any possible way. I think the commission I have suggested in this Bill would be well qualified to fix the standards on those articles mentioned in the Bill, and they would remove any onus from the department or officers connected with the department. The public at large could have every confidence in this commission who had fixed these standards.
There are other clauses which provide that the -commission shall meet twice a year, and that the commission shall be called on notice of the chief analyst for the purpose of considering the advisability of placing some new article on that standard or of changing the present regulation.
Those, Sir, in substance, are the main provisions of this Bill. I trust the Minister of Inland Revenue will take it into his favourable consideration, and will adopt if possible some of its provisions and incorporate them in our present law. At present the standard is fixed under the Adulteration Act, and virtually it is the chief analyst whose duty it is to fix the stand-Mr. J. A. CURRIE.
ards. The Act has been on the statute-book for many years, and we have had no standards as the law says we shall have. The duty of fixing the standards being placed upon the shoulders of one man exposes him possibly to attack from manufacturers on the one hand, and also to attack from the public on the other. For that reason I think the commission as proposed here would lead us wisely out of the difficulty. The Australian law provides for a commission established on a similar basis, and it has received the commendation of those who have given consideration to the matter of pure foods in other countries, and other countries have followed a similar plan. I think, Sir, that the matters dealt with under this Bill are of sufficient importance to the people of Canada to merit that, the Bill should be considered in committee, to see if we cannot arrive at some better method of securing a high quality of foods in this country than we have at present.

Mr. Speaker, it would be premature to discuss the Bill, as explained by the hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Currie), at the present time. When it is printed and circulated and when we have had time to study its provisions it will be the proper time to give that consideration which my hon. friend asks for it. But, as my hon. friend explains the Bill, it seems to me, that we would require to amend or repeal the Adulteration of Foods Act. The most important provision in the Bill, as explained by my'hon. friend, is that providing for the establishment of standards for foods. In the present Adulteration of Foods Act, as my hon. friend has just stated, there is power for the Governor General in Council to establish standards of food and if the Adulteration of Foods Act in Canada has not been that success that it might have been it is due to the fact that standards of food have never been established. But, for some months the chief chemist of the department has had the question under consideration and food standards are now being prepared and_will be in force, under the present Adulteration of Foods Act, I think, on the first of April next. These standards embrace 500 or 600 articles of food. It has been a large undertaking for the chemist of the department to prepare these standards, but I am hopeful that as soon as the manufacturers of food stuffs in Canada and others interested have been apprised of what these standards are going to be, and as soon as the standards are properlv prepared they will be enforced. I just want to state that at the present time under the Adulteration of Foods Act the department is preparing to put into force what is apparently the most important provision of my

hon. friend's Bill. However, after the Bill is printed and circulated we will have a better opportunity of considering it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of *hallways and Canals).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to custom, I propose to make a few observations on the work of the Department of Railways and Canals including that branch of the department's work, so much talked about, the Intercolonial railway. I wish in the beginning to note the regret I feel at the withdrawal from the public service of Mr. Butler, the able deputy and chief engineer of the department. In the few years he has been in the department he has made good, if I may be allowed that expression, and his efficiency in every

branch of his work is acknowledged. But perhaps above and beyond that is the fact that his sterling integrity and unswerving devotion to the public interest are conceded by every person. It is too bad in the public interest that we are not able to retain the services of such men because a question of salary, certainly, in reason, is not to be considered, because the difference between a capable and honest man and one who might lack either one or the other of those qualities, might mean an entire year's salary in one transaction in that department. However, Mr. Butler's ability and knowledge have been recognized by a great corporation, he has engaged with them and will leave the department in a few day3 1 have appointed in his place as deputy minister, Mr. Archibald W. Campbell, who is well known, particularly throughout the province of Ontario. Mr. Campbell is an engineer of standing and for the past few years has been deputy Minister in the Public Works Department of the provincial government. I know Mr. Campbell personally, and he has an excellent reputation, both for ability and honesty, and I believe that in him I have secured a deputy minister who will give good service to the country. I intend to make a change in the officials of my department to the extent that Mr. Campbell will act as deputy minister and a chief engineer will be appointed, separate and apart from the position of deputy minister. I propose also to make Mr. Campbell, chairman of the Board of Management of the Intercolonial railway, of which I shall speak in a few moments.
What will be the difference in cost by reason of dividing the position?

It will depend on the salary I will be compelled to give the new man as chief engineer. Mr. Campbell's salary as deputy is regulated by the Civil Service Act and will be $5,000. Mr. Butler, as chief engineer, receives $3,000 in addition to the $5,000. I may say frankly that I have no anticipation that I can get a chief engineer of the ability required for the position for anything like the difference between $5,000 and $8,000. I propose to look about and see what I can do, and then I shall lay before the House an estimate for the amount for which I think we can get a chief engineer.
What experience has Mr. Campbell had on railways?

Previous deputies of the Department of Railways and Canals have had very little experience in railways, and as deputy he would not need to have any experience in railways other than being a good business man. When the Temiska-Mr. GRAHAM.
ming and Northern Ontario railway, that is the Ontario government railway, was constructed, the construction was undertaken through a commission, and that commission originally was under the Public Works Department of Ontario. The present commission reports through that department. In the original construction, I think Mr. Campbell as deputy-I am speaking from memory-had a good deal to do in the department with the detail of the construction, not of the actual work but of the returns. So fax as I know that is all the experience he has had in railway work.
In approaching the question of transportation, we enter upon a veTy large subject. Canada has undertaken very large things in the way of the solving of the problem of carrying the produce of the people at as fair a rate as possible, but the work that she has begun and has now in contemplation does not by any means mean the completion of what she will have to undertake. I shall not detain the House further than to say what I have said before, that I believe the' Canadian people have shown greater courage than any people in the world in this direction, and that in the years to come and even now, we are reaping the benefit. But the present benefit is nothing to what the people to follow us will reap in this country from the amount of money we are now expending in solving this great question. I look forward to the time/ I think with some degree of reason at least, when Canada will do a large proportion of the carrying trade of this continent. We will not only carry our own goods from west to east and east to west, but will, on account of our situation and the natural advantages we enjoy, be enabled to make a successful bid for a large portion of the carrying trade of our neighbours to the south, because business men accept the best offers they can get for transportation as for anything else; and I say again that I look to the time when Canada will do a large portion of the carrying trade of the continent of America.
I shall not go into generalities, but wish to state a few concrete facts in connection with the work of transportation. During my visit abroad last summer I took occasion to visit the great Kiel canal in Germany. This is, if I remember, the 'only canal in Germany owned by the state, or at least the only large one. The great majority of the canals in Germany and other countries of Europe are owned by private companies. Some of them are owned by county councils, some by railway companies, which is a somewhat anomalous position when we consider the fact that canals are supposed to be rivals of railways and to reduce the cost of transportation. I visited the Kiel canal, a very large work about 61 miles long. It connects the

Baltic sea with the North sea and is used for the transport of the smaller war vessels, and the great improvements being made in it is for the purpose, I believe, of enabling the German government to move their larger warships from ocean to ocean. The length of the locks they propose to .make in the new canal will be approximately 800 feet, and the locks, will be 150 feet wide and 42 feet deep. This is looked upon as a very large enterprise and it is, but, Sir, when we look at some of the enterprises that are staring the Canadian people in the face, I think we might well say that Canada has engineering problems that she has undertaken and others that she will shortly undertake that will compare favourably in magnitude with even the great Kiel canal which the German government is building. The question of smaller canals in Germany is one that is attracting the very close attention of the German government. They have plans now prepared to practically make a network of canals all through the German empire. But, as I said a moment ago, they are not built by the state or the government, they are largely owned by private corporations, and in some instances by county councils. They build them in canalized rivers, they build small canals connecting lakes, and also build them where there seems to be practically no communication, in order, as one gentleman pointed out to me, to give manufacturers an opportunity to extend their operations out on these cheap waterways, away from the cities, away from the larger taxation, and the other troubles that they have in cities. The manufacture of coarser goods, such as brick, &c., is said to be greatly assisted by the construction of these smaller canals.
Did the minister find any like the
-the Newmarket canal?

My hon. friend is getting anxious again. Another point that struck me. and here I think Canada will stand fairly well in the comparison, is that I did not find a canal in the countries I visited owned by any of these people which was free like the Canadian waterways. We have shown greater courage in making our canals free than any of these countries. In Germany, and in England a? well, the rates in many cases were high. On one canal the .rates were five cents a ton besides harbour dues charged for loading and unloading in harbours constructed along the canal. On another canal the rate went to seven cents a ton, and these canals are run both for the benefit of navigation and as investments. In most instances they pay a small interest on the investment. I point
these things out to call attention to the fact that in that respect Canada has shown greater courage than any of these older countries by spending millions upon her canals and throwing them open to the commerce of the North American continent. I also took occasion to visit the great Manchester ship canal, which is about 60 miles from the sea; but even at that distance .Manchester is made an ocean port. But I wish to draw attention to the fact that Montreal is now an ocean port, though a good many miles farther from the ocean than Manchester. We have spent millions of dollars in making Montreal an ocean port, and in that again we have_ shown courage for a young people. Taking our expenditures on our railways, our canals and our waterways generally, it is not at all out of the way to say that Canada has shown greater courage than any other country in the world in the amount of money she has expended per head of the population for carrying out these great works.
With regard to our canals, we have all heard the discussions pro and con upon the Georgian Bay canal and the Welland canal. The opinion of the government as to these is pretty well known. I might state here that there is now being urged the necessity, owing to the great increase in icanal traffic in this country, of building another lock at the Sault. Allow me to make a guess, which will not be considered an educated guess on my part, that this will cost the country from $8,000,000 to $10,000,000. That lock, if constructed, ought to provide for a depth of from 25 to 27 feet, 1 e-cause it wnuld be folly to half do the work, when in a few years we would have either to deepen the lock or build a new one.
A few words of statistical information. The canals of Canada in 1909 carried perhaps the largest volume of traffic in their history. The freight which passed through amounted to 33,720,748 tons, as compared with 17,502,820 in 1908. This was an increase of 16,217,928 tons, or 93 per 'cent in one year. To give an idea of the measure of increase in the freight traffic through our canals, let me state that three years ago the total traffic was only 10,523,185 tons, and ten years ago it was only 5,013,693 tons; so that last year it was nearly seven times as much as it was ten years ago. Of the traffic of 1909, 27,976,399 tons was eastbound and 5,744,349 westbound.
Has the minister the proportions of Canadian and foreign?

I have not the figures, but I can state generally that while we carried a large amount of American traffic, the proportion of increase of Canadian traffic has been equal and perhaps a little more than that of American traffic.

In this connection I may be allowed to call attention to Port Colborne and the Port Colborne elevator. The harbour at that point was originally an open roadstead which was at the mercy of the sea, and it became absolutely necessary to protect the harbour if it was to be used as an entrance to the canal. Both the Public Works Department and the Department of Railways and Canals have done a large amount of work there. That entrance to the canal was adopted a good many years ago. At that time or shortly afterwards the depth of water in the canal was only 14 feet, and, therefore, the depth of the entrance was only 14 feet. But when it became advisable to build an elevator at Port Colborne, to unload the traffic from larger vessels into smaller ones, it became necessary to make the depth of the harbour equal to the draft of the vessels on the lakes. . As the ruling draft of the vessels on the great lakes is now 20 feet, it became necessary to make this harbour suitable for vessels of that draft. This .cost a large amount of money for the protection of the harbour; and I may say that more work will have to be done in the way of building breakwaters in order that the harbour may be fully protected, and that ships may be perfectly safe there, no matter what storms may prevail outside, in taking on or discharging their cargoes. The elevator at Port Colborne has now a capacity of 860,000 bushels, and we have foundations and other provisions for increasing that to 2,000,000 bushels. Last year there was put through that elevator about 1,500,000 bushels. That is a comnaratively small quantity, particularly when you bear in mind that this elevator is perhaps as efficient a one as can be found any where, capable of unloading some 60,000 bushels per hour. I was not at all sanguine that this elevator, if carried on by the government, .would handle any great amohnt of grain. I think it is no secret that corporations only use government property when they cannot do anything else. They do not encourage us to any great extent in this work. But I am told by a very large shipper that the fact that there was such an elevator at Port Colborne, ready and willing to tranship .grain from the larger vessels into the smaller ones, had a very mollifying influence on the freight rates by other routes. One man thought that this resulted in a saving of nearly a cent a bushel in the rates of the other transportation lines. I am not going to discuss that, because I dc not know. But even if the saving were onlv half a cent or a quarter of a cent a bushel, it would mean a great dear to the people shipping their grain from the west. It might be in the interest of all parties- I have not made up my mind on it-if the Mr. GRAHAM.
elevator were leased and run in connection with some of the lines of transportation; but if we did that, unless some restrictions were imposed, it might deprive us of the benefit the elevator now confers of keeping down the freight rates on other routes.
Leaving the canals, allow me to take up the question of the railways of Canada. We have a larger railway mileage per head of the population than any other country in the world. It now amounts to 24,104 miles, an increase on the previous year of 1,138 miles. There is a peculiar situation in reference to the traffic of last year: there was a considerable improvement in the moving of products, but the passenger traffic fell off. Notwithstanding the apparent improvement in business, the people did not travel as much last year as the year before when business was better, perhaps having less business they had more time to travel the year before. ' The results were as follows:
The railway mileage of Canada' is now 24,104, an increase of 1,138 miles during the year.
The freight traffic aggregated 66,842,258 tons, an increase of 3,771,091 tons. In dollars $1,9G8,128.00.	.
The passenger traffic amounted to 32,683,309, a decrease of 1,361,683. A decrease in dollars of $919,015.00.
Nearly a million dollars decrease in the income from the carrying of passengers last year. I do not attempt to explain it but merely state the fact.

From the point 597 miles west of the Wolf creek to Prince Rupert, a distance of 2401
miles, the work of grading and the construction of wooden bridges is under contract with Messrs. Foley, Welch and Stewart.
No work has as yet been executed on the first 40 miles, and merely a good start has been made on. the next 100 miles; the reasons being, that navigation closed on the Skeena river about a month earlier than usual, thus putting a stop to running in supplies, tools, plant, etc. However, the contractors are exerting their efforts to push a tote road through so as to enable them to haul in supplies, etc., by team and keep the. work moving throughout the winter. They ore now at work on one of the tunnels and some rock cuttings.
The work of grading and the construction of wooden bridges on the last 100 miles, to Prince Rupert, was practically completed when a very heavy storm with a high tide caused damage, washing away some of the rock embankments where exposed to the sweep of the open ocean, and bringing down considerable slides from the mountain sides, filling up some cuttings and blocking up waterways. The damage, however, was not very extensive.
Mr. Ferguson, the contractor for the sub structure of the several steel bridges, having failed in carrying out his contract, the Grank Trunk Pacific Railway Company have relieved him of the work, and are carrying it on themselves by day labour. This work is progressing very slowly, but better conditions are promised for the future. If these promises are not realized, the track-laying in the spring will be delayed.
Steel rails for this 100 miles; one locomotive; one conductors' van and 24 cars, for the work of track-laying and ballasting, have been delivered at Prince Rupert, and a large quantity of ties have been delivered along the line.
About one mile of track has been laid, but nothing further will be done in that direction until next spring.

Now, Sir, I come to a very important matter. Hon. gentlemen have no doubt read with some interest the report presented by Mr. Butler, chief engineer and Deputy Minister of the Department of Railways, on the Hudson bay route. This report was made by Mr. Butler after studying the report of Mr. Armstrong, the engineer in _ charge of the Hudson bay railway project. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make it clear to the country and clear to this House that this government has been committed to this work and intends to proceed with it with all possible speed. After a full study of the matter, or rather a study of it so far as is possible at the present time, the government has decided, and I believe the country will concur in that decision, that it is advisable to make the Hudson bay route another great outlet for the rapidly increasing products of the western part of this great country. Every dollar that can be saved to the people of the west in the transportation of their products means that a large part of that dollar will go to better remunerate
them for the labour they expend in the cultivation of the land. The government intends to proceed as rapidly as possible with the construction of this work. You will notice in the report presented by Mr. Butler something which no doubt surprised many hon. members, as it certainly did surprise me. I refer to the fact that in the opinion of Mr. Armstrong, the engineer, Nelson harbour is superior to Churchill as the terminus of the Hudson bay railroad. I had always concluded, whether rightly or wrongly, that Churchill was the most suitable harbour on the Hudson bay, but my preconceived idea in that respect has been upset by the report of Mr. Armstrong, who, from the data secured, has no hesitation in expressing his opinion that Nelson is the better harbour of the two.
Which would be the shorter route?
To Nelson it is 67 miles shorter than to Churchill, by the railroad.
Has he given his reasons why he believes Nelson is the better harbour?
They are explained very well in the report.
I drew a different conclusion from the report of the same man.

Well, he says in his report that Nelson is the better harbour. However, before either terminus is selected it would be wise to make sure of that fact, and I may say that the Minister of Marine will ask from the House a vote for the purpose of sending a ship up through the channel which will come into both these harbours from the outside, make an examination of the channel and of the passage through the straits. This expedition will make a thorough investigation of the entrance to the outer harbours of both places, and when that is done we v7ill be in a position to take up in a more practical way that part of the project at the harbour end. But that need not mean any delay in the beginning of the construction of the railway. Included in this great project there are wharfs and elevators, and the construction of these great . wharfs and elevators will be greatly facilitated by having the railway constructed so that the material may be carried in. I repeat that the delay necessary in making a full investigation as to the particular harbour which will be selected does not of necessity mean delay in the construction of the railway which, in my opinion, ought to. be constructed in advance of the building - of the elevators and wharfs, so that the supplies may be more economically taken on the ground.
Instead of sending a ship round there to take soundings in the harbour, why not send a canoe? It would do just as well.
It is not far from the strait into the harbour, and the ship will be sent to make observations in the Strait as well.
That is a different matter.
The ship will enter the harbours of Churchill and Nelson and make observations and give us information as to the approaches to these harbours as well as with respect to the conditions inside.

The approach to the straits would be the same for one harbour as for the other, and I see no reason whatever for delaying to get up a junketing expedition to explore the harbours. There are fifty boats plying along each harbour, and the soundings of these harbours are just as well known as the soundings of the harbour of Montreal.

I am glad my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) has information Mr. GRAHAM.
about that, because the engineers have divergent views.
The minister had that information in his department long years ago.

Well, I will not stop to discuss that now. The objection taken to some works undertaken by the government has been that the government embarked on the enterprise before they had full information, and so in this case I am going to try and get information in order that we may ensure that rve shall select the proper harbour.
'Does the hon. gentleman propose to start to build his railway before he knows where the terminus is going to be? Surely he will want to know in what direction he is going to run the railway.
For over 200 miles the route will be in common no matter which harbour is selected.
Why were not the investigations in regard to the channel made before?

I am sure I do not know why they have not been made before, but, if we are going to provide what is to be a through route, and if we are going to have a railway to connect with, that route for the transportation of the products of the people of the west, I think every one will agree that we ought to have all the information which it is possible for us to obtain as to which is the better harbour. Heretofore the general opinion has been that Churchill is the better harbour, but we are now told by the engineers that Nelson is better, and even if Nelson is no more than as good a harbour as Churchill, if we can save 67 miles railway construction by going to that harbour, I think the country will consider that we are wise in making a thorough investigation of the matter. However, as I have pointed out, that does not mean that we should delay commencing the construction of the railway, because about 260 miles of the road will be the same no matter whiph harbour is selected, namely, from Pas Mission to Split lake.
How far is it from the Pas Mission to Nelson?

It is 410 miles from the Pas Mission to Nelson, and 477 miles from the Pas Mission to Churchill, which gives a difference of 67 miles. There is a very interesting statement in this report, if it be true, that by the construction of this railroad and the establishing of the route, 5 cents per bushel can be saved to the people of the west on the grain they produce. An

examination of the conditions seems to lend credence to that statement, and if that be so it is in the interest of the people, of the west, yes, it is in the interest of Canada as a whole that we should without delay place within the reach of our western people this method of transportation which will enable them to effect this great saving. The report states that the distance from Nelson to Liverpool is 3,200 miles, and from Montreal to Liverpool 3,007 miles, or practically the same distance.
Would the construction of this Hudson bay route have any effect on the Georgian bay canal project?
There is lots of work for both.

It is a little hard to say what the result would he, but I am such an optimist that I believe that within the next 25 years, in the Dominion of Canada, we can undertake to build all the projects we have in view and still not have any too many lines of transportation to carry the products of the country.
If you take grain by the Hudson bay route at 5 cents per bushel to the shipper, I do not see that you will get much advantage the other way.

It was estimated at 5 cents per bushel in comparison with existing rates, and my hon. friend must remember that running the Hudson Bay railway at full steam, and carrying all it is possible, we can relieve the pressure on the traffic from the Northwest to only a small amount, in view of the vast production of that country. I suppose hon. gentlemen have read that report, and they have seen that it is stated as the opinion of Mr. Butler that the coal of eastern Canada could by that route be taken at a commercial price to at least some of the points in the great west. If that be true, then not only is the west interested in the construction of this great work, but the people away in the remote east of Canada are also interested in the rapid and speedy completion of this great railway transportation. Now, without going into further details, I may say that when the supplementary estimates come down there will be an item providing for the commencement of the construction of this project as rapidly as possible, and I hope during the coming summer; I believe we will be able to undertake the construction of this project this summer, before we have another session of parliament. The country can rest assured that the government proposes to deal with this work in a practical way, and to proceed with its construction; because if any benefit is to accrue, I have
always believed in trying to get some of it for the people who are now doing the work and making the investment, and the sooner we get this project completed, the sooner returns will come to the people.
What is the estimated cost of the railway?

The engineer in charge, Mr. Armstrong, made an estimate, and the chief engineer of my department thought that in his estimate he had not provided for a standard of road such as ought to be constructed for the heavy traffic that will be carried during the very busy season. I want to say that this estimate is made on preliminary surveys, a survey party is now engaged in making the location from Le Pas to Split lake. There may be an increase in this figure after the line is properly located, because an estimate that may be approximate on a preliminary survey quite often is not a proper estimate if you have to change the location to some other point, and make it an absolute location. The estimate as given for the entire railway, with elevators, warehouse and terminal facilities at Nelson, is $16,426,340.
Is that likely to be as accurate as the Grand Trunk Pacific estimate?

I have tried to explain these estimates to the House. I say frankly that these are approximate, because these are not location surveys, and we might run across a different kind of soil, and different material. But this provides for a railway of a grade of four-tenths of one per cent. There may be some difference of opinion as to the necessity of building a road with 80-lb. rails and an expensive grade of that kind. But as a matter of fact, the contour of the country is nearly level, and the engineer thinks he is well within his estimate.
Four tenths of one per cent going to Hudson bay?
The engineer thinks it is practicable to make a grade of that kind both ways, and that grade will be at least for the east bound traffic.
Is the western end to commence at Le Pas mission and run into the prairie country?

The western end of this line has always been discussed and regarded as starting from Le Pas mission. Provision can be made for running lines into the country in other directions, but the western end of this line is supposed

to commence at what is known as Le Pas mission.
Is it the idea of the government to construct this as a government work?

The hon. gentleman is asking me questions very rapidly. There might be a difference of opinion as to whether this should be constructed as a government work, or whether we should allow the project to be dealt with largely by a company. To-day I am not prepared to say in what way it may ultimately be done. But no matter how it is done, that does not of necessity mean that we cannot begin the construction at once, because if "an arrangement were made with a company that was satisfactory, any work the government had done could be handed over to it on reasonable terms in a contract..

The minister has said that there will be an appropriation in the supplementary estimates for building the Hudson Bay railway. I would like to know if ' there is any chance of an amount being provided for the commencement of the Georgian Bay canal?

Well, I think not this year. I have not been discussing the Georgian Bay canal. However, it is a great work which is before the people, and will be constructed in due time b.y this government, which has always undertaken the great projects that the country required. Now, Sir, the question of what a railway ought to do has been discussed in this House, and discussed elsewhere. Some hon. gentlemen have thought that a railway is a great promoter of industry, that is, that a railway can own industries, run them and make them profitable, and thus develop the country. I think however, that is hardly the proper view to take. As for England, I have looked into a recent decision there which was to the effect, that a railway company could not engage in any other business, but it must devote itself to the business of transportation. But there are cases in the old land where railways have constructed canals and operated them in connection with the railway. I think that is not the best method, because it places the rates practically in the hands of one company, and canals do not operate as they ought to operate in keeping down railway rates. But returning to the question of railways doing other business, in England they are not allowed to transact other business. In France, I think six private companies own all the railways except that portion of the railways that is owned Mr. GRAHAM.
by the state, the figures of which I will give in a few minutes. The conditions of aid given to the French railways are such that, if carried out, the state will own all the French railways by 1950 or 1960. But it is fair to say that as occasion requires, France has deviated from the arrangement with those railways, and has made some concessions and changed the conditions that were originally made. The only railway line not being operated under this arrangement with the government, was recently taken over by the French government, I think they call it the Great West Railway, which is now a part of the system. In the United States, one of the troubles in connection with railways during the past few years has been that they have been doing a coal business in connection with the railway, and imposing rates that the people thought were too high. When the Interstate Commerce Commission took charge, they began regulating the rate of the railways, but the railway could immediately proceed to make it up on the price of coal, and consequently there was no benefit coming to the people from the regulation of that railway. The inter-state commerce law now prohibits railways from owning and operating coal mines. If they do it they have to do it under some other name. I am merely pointing this out to show that the theory that a railway could go into any part of Canada and operate coal mines would not work out to the benefit of the people, and it would not be five years until an Act was passed prohibiting that because we would lose in railway rates by such an amalgamation. The United States has found it necessary to say that railways shall not own and operate coal mines.
I wish to place before the House a short statement in reference to the state railways of the continent of Europe to which I have given some study during the past few months. Germany, out ;of 35,000 miles, operates 31,043. In answer to my hon. friend I want to point out that the federal government of Germany does not own a mile of railway, but that these railways are owned and operated by the various states in Germany, just as if the various provinces in Canada owned and operated their railways. So, it is hardly fair to point to German state railways and compare the situation there to that which would exist in Canada if Canada owned her railways. I wish to say again that the states of the German empire own and operate their railways and that the federal government does not, while in Canada it would be the federal government that would have to operate them. In Victoria the South Australian railway is operated under a commission, being 1,879 miles in length, while in New Zealand 2,682 miles of railway'are owned and operated by the government under a general manager. I may say in passing that in Italy in 1885, owing to dissatisfaction with government operation, the lines were leased to a private company, but they found that private operation was obnoxious, the state took them back in 1905 and they are now being operated by the state.
I could speak at some length on the question of the railways in Germany or with reference to those to which I gave particular attention. I think perhaps it would not be amiss to speak of one or two points. With reference to passenger rates on all railways, I think I am safe in saying that in the aggregate they are lower than in this country. The great majority of people do not travel first-class on any of the European railways. Asked why the traffic was gradually and constantly increasing. the reason given by one of the general managers was that the multiplicity and increasing number of automobiles rendered it so easy for people who would travel first-class to reach their destinations, in comparatively small countries, that a great many of them travelled bv automobile instead of going by the railway. But, the fact remains that first-class rates are very high in comparison with second or third class rates. On a German railway I travelled from Kiel to Paris, a small portion of the railway being in Fiance, and I paid, first-class, including baggage-and it was very light baggage-4i cents per mile.
Single fare?
Single fare. I also paid for sleeping accommodation $3.50. When we compare this with our first-class fare it would be abnormally high both for the sleeping accommodation and the travelling rate.
Was that an upper berth?

No, this was a good berth. The accommodation is excellent on the trains, but I submit again that there are certain phases of travel in the old land, even in a first-class carriage, or in a good many of them, that are not as good as they are in this country. An improvement is being made and has been made during the past few years, by the introduction of corridor cars, which removes to a large extent some of the objections which I have in mind. Go where you will in the old land, whether on a private or a state owned line, and you are impressed with the fact that first-class travellers have to pay much more than they do in this country. In Germany they practically carry no baggage at all, or a very small amount, and you have to pay for your baggage. That may account for the other fact that people coming from Germany or from the old land carry into their seats all the baggage they possibly can because they have got into the habit of having their baggage weighed in England or weighed and paid for in Germany. When you come to the lower classes, travelling is very cheap in the old land, and it can be cheap because there passengers travel by the million and the railways have the short haul and the crowded trains which is the ideal condition enabling a railway to make money. But, when you come to freight it is a little different. I found this out in my investigation, and I came back impressed with the fact that there is no place in Europe, at least, where the control over rates can at all compare with the eontrol over rates by the government of this country. They have control, through certain bodies, over the rates, but their rules are so lenient and their enforcement is, I think, so lax, that the railway companies, as far as I could judge, practically make their own rates and have very little, if any, interference. A good deal has been said in this country about cheaper passenger fares. That is the ideal situation, but I submit to the House and the country that the people whose labour is involved in the producing of goods are more interested in getting cheap rates for the transport of their goods than they are in securing cheaper passenger rates.
That is that the human consideration is less than the dead matter.

The consideration is not as my hon. friend stated. It is a matter of dollars and cents, but the human consideration is also taken into account. The matter of dollars and cents comes back all the same to the man's pocket whether he

is travelling himself or sending a carload of freight.
There are some things you cannot measure in dollars and cents

That is true, and it is a good thing it is true. When I come 'to consider the freight situation I say without hesitation that the people of Canada are in an infinitely better position as regards freight rates and the amount they get for the money paid in freight rates than they are in any country in Europe. I will in a few moments give you a table of figures which, I think, will convince you of that fact. The great attention paid to passenger rates in the old land seems to have deterred them from going as far as they might with respect to freight traffic. Of course, they have the small cars, wagons they call them, of 15 or 20 tons, although some, I think, are now 30 tons. But when you come to consider the freight rates they have to pay on this haulage, the people of this country would be astonished. In Germany, with state owned railways, taking into consideration all the special rates-and they have many of them-the freight in that great country of industry, that country filled with population and teeming with the products of the people, are more than double what we pay in Canada. In the matter of freight haulage we in Canada,-owing possibly to the regulation by the commission, and to the fact that we have given much aid to the companies-have rates lower than are enjoyed in any country in Europe which I visited. Speaking of the Railway Commission, I was called on by two or three gentlemen in London and was told that we were giving altogether too much power to our board of railway commissioners. One gentleman said that we were going so far as to perhaps make capital a little timid. Of course, I disagreed with him at once, and took up, as I thought, the practical side, the benefit derived by the people on account of the appointment of the commission and the1 work they are carrying out. I believe to-day that the decisions of the commission are fair and that the commission are looking after the interests of the people, but not in a way to be unjust to the men who have put their money into these great undertakings. The people of Canada do not want any control to be unjust to the people who have made investments in this country, and I do not believe the commissioners are unjust.
Have any data been collected as to the possibility of winter navigation as apart from the spring navigation of Hudson straits?

I cannot perhaps give my hon. friend a satisfactory answer. My idea in having a steamer sent up there would he that we would make observations and get all the data necessary. That is the reason why I thought great care would have to be exercised. I have read in reports that while the navigation in the harbour was open for quite a long period, the navigation in the Strait vims open for a much shorter period. These questions only emphasize the necessity of a thorough investigation before we decide on what harbour we should select.
I turn now to another question involved in the management of the Department of Railways and Canals, that is the Quebec bridge. Hon. gentlemen will excuse me, I know, for giving a brief history of this project since it was taken over by the Department of Railways and Canals two years ago, and the work of preparing for reconstruction undertaken. As there are a good many technical terms in connection with this, the House will bear with me if I read the memoranda because some hon. gentlemen in the House are engineers and they will like to see the statement just as it is. The memorandum is as follows:

Following the precedent of the United States government in the case of the Panama canal; the state of New York in the case of the Erie Canal enlargement; and of the city of New York in the case of the Blackwell's Island bridge, a board of eminent engineers has been appointed charged with the responsibility of designing the bridge, and the following gentlemen were selected for the task:-
Henri Vautelet, M. Can. Soc. C. E., of Montreal, as chairman and chief engineer.
Ralph Modjeski, M. Am. Soc. C. E., consulting engineer, of Chicago.
Maurice Fitzmaurice, C. M. G., M. Inst. C. E., chief engineer, London county council, England.
The task entrusted to these gentlemen is a great one, and, as was anticipated at the time of their appointment, material differences of opinion have arisen between them. Under the provisions of the order in council creating the board, in the event of differences arising, consulting engineers were to be called in to assist. Accordingly, on the question of foundations and substructures, Mr. Alfred Noble, M. Am. Soc. C. E., chief engineer of the Pennsylvania Railway tunnel, of New York (one of the most experienced men in America in foundation work), and Mr. Henry Holgate, M. Can. Soc C. E., of Montreal, were selected, and the matters in dispute were accordingly settled.
The south pier is to be enlarged to an area of 180 feet by 80 feet at the base.
A new caisson is to be sunk for the north pier and is to be carried to the rock, reducing the span from 1,800 to 1,785 feet.
Specifications covering every phase of the substructure work have been completed. Gen-

eral plans for guidance of the contractors have been prepared. The work of the substructure was advertised widely and the work was allotted to Messrs. M. P. & J. T. Davis, they being the lowest tenderers.
The other tenderers were Larkin & Sangster and M. Connolly.
Superstructure.
A great deal of valuable work has been done. The span, centre to centre of main piers, has been fixed at 1,758 feet; the width, centre to centre of trusses, at 88 feet; with a maximum depth of truss of 290 feet. A clear head room of 150 feet above the highest water has been provided for, a width of 600 feet under the centre of the bridge.
A general specification has been prepared, fixing the loading so that it will be ample for all possible contingencies of the future.
The unit stresses allowed have been settled, for carbon steel and nickel steel, and are conservative.
The form of the main compression members has been determined.
A series of tests of model columns has been started and a similar series of tests of chord bars will be carried to completion.
The dead load has been thoroughly computed and the relative concentrations determined, thus eliminating all possibility of error in calculations for the new structure.
Material differences of opinions relating to the superstructure have arisen from time to time between members of the board, and acting under the provision of the order in council, Mr. Paul Wolfel, M. Am. Soc. C. E., consulting engineer of Philadelphia, and Mr. Phelps Johnson, chief engineer and manager of the Dominion Bridge Company, of Montreal, were called in as consulting engineers, and the difficulties were overcome.
The work has advanced and at present stage is as follows:-
An advertisement has been published in the ' London Engineering ' and ' The Engineer/ in England; 'The New York Engineering News' and 'The Engineering Record,' in New York; and in the Canadian press, inviting the bridge builders of the world to go to the office of the board at Montreal and study the problem. The plans and general specifications are here, and they will be allowed until May to prepare their studies, get familiar with the details of the plans and specifications; after that date three or four months will be allowed for the preparation of tenders. All tenderers must bid on the plans prepared by the board, but may submit alternative designs-in this way the form of the trusses, about which there is a reasonable difference of opinion, will be tested; the question of a suspension or cantilever bridge will be settled. 1 he board have completed studies for a suspension bridge and also for a single intersection cantilever. The ultimate decision will be made when all the designs are before the board, having regard to: first, safety; second, speed of erection and completion; third, cost.
As the responsibility for the proper carrying on of the work is placed upon the builder, and the fact that the best designs the board are able to prepare is in competition with the best efforts of the best bridge builders in the world, we hope to secure the best bridge that the present state of engineering skill can produce.

Davis, -who secured the contract for piers, was the lowest tenderer, the other tenderers being Messrs. Larkin & Sangster and Mr. Connolly.
I wish to point out to the House, although perhaps it is unnecessary, that unless you have studied this question beside an engineer and listened to all the difficulties suggested and discussed by him, or you are an engineer yourself, you have no idea of the magnitude of this work. It is so great that men with the ability and the reputation of these men will only move very carefully and very cautiously and not until they have absolutely made a study of every step to be taken. As I pointed out to them when discussing the question with them, the great point to be considered was the stability of this project, there must be no chance, so far as engineering skill can provide against such chance, of any failure in the construction and the remaining constructed of this bridge. That being their instructions-and they would have done it without any such instructions -they studied every step with the greatest care, tests and studies were made both in this country, in the United States and in more than one country in the old world, so that step by step they might be sure of what they were doing.
The effect of the specification as to width and height of the bridge, mentioned in the statement I have read, is that the channel for navigation will be 600 feet wide, and that there will be a clear head of 150 feet from the bridge to high water level.

I wish to ask the minister whether they had considered the large boats that are liable to come up to Montreal. Some years ago I had occasion to place some statistics and facts in regard to the boats coming across the Atlantic, and I would like to know whether it is not possible to raise the bridge more than 150 feet above the water.

That matter was placed before this board and information obtained and discussed, but it was thought that if any vessel needed a greater space than that for its masts or funnels, provision should be made for passing the bridge in the construction of the ship, but in all human probability this 150 feet will accommodate all vessels that want to come to Montreal.
Not with the Marconi system; it will only allow the smokestacks to go under.
Has the minister at hand a statement of the differences between the engineers as to the substructure, to settle which these other engineers were called in?

The trouble was techni-cal2 so technical that I would not attempt to explain it. It was a difference between engineers. The question came up about formations and finding solid rock. Another term I heard discussed was as to the angle of repose for the earth-how far they would have to go to get certain results. There were technical questions of engineering, and these two experts were called in to consult with them. I might say that it is proposed that in the contract with the builder, so that there can be no question, he shall be required to accept the contract on the plans and specifications, and shall be held responsible as a builder for the construction of the bridge on the plans and specifications which he accepts.
Will he have a guarantee?
He will have to give a guarantee or he cannot get the contract.

Leaving that and coming to a question of more local interest, perhaps, I will take up the much-discussed, mildly-criticised and somewhat interesting question of the Intercolonial railway. I want to speak of the question of capital account in connection with railways. The Intercolonial railway management, both under this government and under previous governments, has been criticised for its expenditure on capital account. Some of the criticisms, possibly, have been fair, but some of it I think will not be warranted by a comparison with other road3. A great advance has been made in arriving at a basis of what should be charged to capital account in the last few years owing to the action of the Interstate Commerce Commission. Under the ruling of that commission, a certain amount each year, according to the particular railway, is required to be devoted to betterments, and any betterments over and above this stated amount must come out of capital. That is to prevent work being done out of revenue that ought to be done out of capital. The result of the former method, or lack of method, was that in good fat years, when there was good business, the companies would make a lot of expenditures out of their revenue. That would really prevent the public knowing what their net profits were. But since the Interstate Commerce Commission have endeavoured to regulate rates, they have insisted that many things which heretofore were charged to revenue, shall be charged to capital account, so that people will know exactly what the profits of the railway companies are, and they can regulate their rates accordingly. I know that is the reverse of the argument that has been used, but that is the absolute fact to-day under the ruling of the Inter3tate Commerce Commission. If we take the principle that is now adopted on all the American railways, the Intercolonial can stand side by side with them on a question of what should be charged to capital and what to revenue. I will go further: I believe that in past years we have charged to revenue what under the Interstate Commerce law we would be compelled to charge to capital.
And vice versa?

There is no vice versa in this case. On the question of what ought to be charged to capital account there has been a difference of opinion. I have been told in this House that certain small expenditures should not be charged to capi-

tal account, and that when a railway reaches a certain point its capital account ought to cease.
The minister speaks of the Interstate Commerce Commission controlling capital account. When does he propose that the Railway Commission of Canada shall have similar control?

That is a question to be dealt with by the Canadian parliament, of which my hon. friend is a member. I admit that I think he has done his duty in that respect. We want to treat the government railways in as approximately fair a way as we would the railway of a company. This much seems to be forgotten that about seventy-five per cent of the company lines on this continent have gone into liquidation, and the original capital and the original stock-holders have, for all purposes of profit, been wiped out. If you would apply the same principle to the Intercolonial railway, you could have wiped out all the capital invested in it some years ago, and started afresh, just as the purchasers of these other railways did when they wiped out the original investment by legal sale. Every dollar invested on capital account on the Intercolonial railway stands there to-day against it, whereas in many of the company lines one-half the original capital has been practically wiped out by liquidation.
It is said sometimes that the Intercolonial railway charges small things to capital which should come out of revenue. Well, in that respect I submit the Intercolonial stands on all fours with company lines and will also compare with them in that same respect as regards age. If the capital account of a railway must cease after a number of years, then the Baltimore and Ohio, which is 82 years old, ought to have come nearly to the end of its capital account. But it has not. I have its last annual report before me; and I find in that report charged to capital account items of a similar kind as those objected to in the capital account of the Intercolonial Tailway. For instance, I find such items as repairing tracks at shops, $289.18; a wagon scale, $358.62; new track scale, $983.69; improving track crossing, $98.23; new stock block, $142.44; sidings, new yardmaster's office, increasing water supply, new yards, round house-all these items are very familiar, and we see them all in the capital account of the Baltimore and Ohio railway as presented last year in its 82nd annual report. Therefore, the Intercolonial railway is doing exactly what these companies are doing as regards expenditure on capital account.

What I would like for my own information is not so much the in-90

If we could have those principles, which have now become operative in the United States, under the commission my hon. friend speaks of, explained by the minister, that would be of real service to the .House. In the case of a round house or a yardmaster's house, several things might occur. Was the track-master's house to replace one which had been burnt down or was it a new building rendered necessary for the traffic of the road and, therefore, chargeable to capital?
The report says a new yardmaster's office
Whether the yardmaster was new or not, I suppose the house was one which had not existed before and was not the successor of a similar house.

I am not sure whether the yardmaster was new or not. It was the office I was speaking of, and my hon. friend was simply making a little play on words. The items in the Baltimore and Ohio report are identical with those we have in our own capital account. The rule, I think, is that anything which will add to the value of the property, any betterment which will add to the power of earning, should go into capital account. One man, a very great authority, has given the extreme opinion that if you put two nails into a plank where there was only one before, the second should be charged to capital account.
So that is the principle, we can understand it.

I have given it in my own words.

The American roads, through the commission, are systematizing the whole business of capitalization and keeping accounts. It would be useful information if we could get the actual rules and principles adopted in that country.
I think that would be a good idea, and I thought I had explained it.

As the hon. gentleman has put it, if you put an additional nail in a plank along side the one which was already there, and it is serviceable, you can charge that additional nail to capital account. But if the old nail rusted out and you put a new one in its place that would not be a new nail and could not be charged to capital account. Is that the ministerial interpretation?

I did not give the Interstate Commerce Commission rule, but I gave the opinion of a railway authority. Practically speaking, anything that is new and that gives additional value or additional earning power is chargeable to capital account.
Suppose a nail rusted out and you put another one in to take its place, that gives additional earning power, as the earning power would be less without it.

I wish to speak for a moment of the Prince Edward Island railway. The Prince Edward Island railway forms no part of the Intercolonial railway. It is run on Prince Edward Island, some 260 miles. I wish to take the House into my confidence clearly in reference to it and to state that you need not expect, it is not fair fo expect, and nobody does expect, that the Prince Edward Island railway will ever keep even. The traffic is not there to keep it even, and we are prepared and must he prepared to run the Prince Edward Island railway for the accommodation of the people and to take out of the consolidated revenue fund of the Department of Canals whatever deficit there may be, because deficit there will be every year no matter what you do so long as you give the people any service at all. Small boats run around the island carrying a large part of the traffic and the island railway serves the people as best it can. I have a good deal of sympathy with the complaint made on Prince Edward Island that they do not get the passenger service that they might expect, not that they do not get all the passenger service to which they are entitled if you discuss it on the cold calculation of what the revenue would warrant, because on that calculation we might not have any service or not have an efficient service. But it is a matter for serious consideration if we ought not to improve the passenger service on the island a trifle and be prepared,
owing to the difficulties that exist there and the isolation of the people, to take out of the consolidated fund of the Dominion of Canada an amount sufficient to give to the people of that island decent and fair passenger service. The members from the island have been urging strongly the construction of branch lines, and branch lines will probably have to be constructed, but that will be a matter for future consideration. I want, however, to place myself absolutely on record as having great sympathy with the people on the island on account of the conditions that exist and to ask the House that when we come to discuss the railway problem as affecting that island, they will not discuss it along distinctly and absolutely business lines, because if you do you will not serve the people of Prince Edward Island as they ought to be served with railway facilities. A great deal has been said as to the rates on the Intercolonial railway. It has been pointed out that the rates of the Intercolonial railway to St. John are the same as those of the Canadian Pacific railway, although the haul is 200 miles longer. The rates to competing points are always the same; but I want to point out that where there is no competition the rates on company owned roads are higher than those on the government road, where there is no competition. Moreover, I want to ask hon. gentlemen from Quebec and Ontario, and especially hon. members from the western part of Canada, if they think, from their experience in the west, that if any private company had had during all these years in the eastern part of Canada the monopoly which the government railway has had, the people would not have paid at least two and a half times as high freight rates as they have been called on to pay on the government road? That means millions in the pockets of the people of the eastern provinces, and millions also in the pockets of the people who have had to transport goods on the government railway when there was no competition. The good which that railway has been to Canada cannot be estimated "by a casual or superficial investigation, but must be estimated by regarding it as a part of the great transportation system of the country and as a regulator of railway rates during the years before we had a railway commission. I believe the Intercol-I onial railway is run as well as any other

railway in this country. For the traffic given,_ I believe it runs a greater number of trains and stops at a greater number of stations and gives greater accommodation to travellers than people could hope to get from any company railway in the world.
How do the passenger and freight rates on the Intercolonial railway compare with the rates on railways in Quebec and Ontario?

The freight rates on the Intercolonial railway, where it has no opposition, are much lower than the rates on comnany roads where they have no competition. The passenger rates, I think, approximate those of other railways throughout Canada.
What about freight rates?
Where the road has a monopoly, they are less on the Intercolonial railway; but from competing points they are exactly the same.
How do they compare with the rates fixed by the commission?

The rates allowed by the commission are higher than the rates on the Intercolonial railway; and if a company had the Intercolonial railway, the commission would allow it to charge higher rates than the Intercolonial railway charges.

He has not told the House what is to be his policy hereafter in regard to the Intercolonial railway. I gather that he is more than half a believer in government _ ownership. In view of the observations he has made in Europe, and in view of the statements going throughout the country that the Intercolonial railway may be abandoned as a state-owned road, what is to be the future of that railway?

That is a pretty broad question, and would bring us to a discussion of the policy of public-owned versus private-owned railways. Conditions sometime arise that alter situations, or situations arise that alter conditions. But I may say to my hon. friend that there is no immediate danger of this road going to a private company, for I purpose continuing the .road under the board of management, and I want to tell the House that I intend to appoint another member to that board in the next few weeks, which I think will be in the interest of the public and of the railway.

Now, I have detained the House too long, for which I must apologize; but I have endeavoured to place before the House and the country the general position of Canada as regards her canals, her railways and the other great projects which we have in hand. I have devoted particular attention to our public-owned railway, the operation of which during the past nine months has shown good results, and which I believe, with the co-operation of those interested in it, such as we have had during the last nine months, will continue to give the people a first-class service at fair rates, and come out at the end of the twelve months without showing a deficit.

I propose to follow the Minister of Railways briefly through the various^ points in connection with the Intercolonial railway which he touched on this afternoon. In the compliments which the hon. minister paid his deputy, Mr. Butler, on the retirement of the latter from office, I heartily concur. In anything I have had to do with Mr. Butler, I always found him very kind and obliging and everything that an [DOT] officer of the government ought to be, and I cordially join the minister in wishing him every success in his new employment. Mr. Butler's successor, the hon. minister has told iis, was formerly Deputy Minister of Public Works in Ontario. Mr. Campbell may be very competent for the office, but personally I know nothing of his qualifications, and we have been told by the minister that he intends appointing also a chief engineer who will take the engineering duties off Mr. Campbell's hands.
On the question of transportation, the hon. minister cited the different kinds in which this country is interested, and spoke of some new schemes which he considered were in the public interest. He passed slightly over the Welland canal and had very little to say in favour of what is, flo my mind, a solution of the transportation problem for the Dominion. I refer to the Georgian bay canal. The Hudson Bay railway scheme, he said, the government were committed to, and he believed that great benefit would result from its completion to the people of the Northwest by the saving on the cost of transportation of their produce. He was of the opinion that the large quantities of grain exported from

that country would yield an additional revenue to the farmers, through the construction of this railway, to the extent of five cents per bushel. Well, Mr. Speaker, the Hudson bay railway scheme was one of the first considered when I entered this House some 37 years ago. I am glad to see it become a practical issue at present, for I was one of the promoters of that scheme. There were then two rival schemes. The promoters of the one declared that the only port worth going to was Fort Churchill, and their rivals advocated the claims of Port Nelson. The Hon. Wm. MacDougall was the promoter of one of the schemes, and I was backing the other. After thorJ outghly -considering the wihole question, after reading with interest the accounts of all the voyages made by British officers to Hudson bay, and all the reports of the Hudson bay schooners which had navigated those waters for the last thirty or forty years, we came to the conclusion that the bay was navigable during a certain portion of the year. How long I do not know. The length varied according to the different seasons. I see that the minister quotes in his report a paper by Mr. Armstrong, who advocates Port Nelson as a terminus, much preferring it to Fort Churchill. Mr. Armstrong says that the bay never freezes over at Fort Nelson during the whole season, that the navigation there is a month longer than it is at Fort Churchill, and still another month longer if you go further south. In that connection I would draw the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) to the statement of Mr. Armstrong, who advocates Port Nelson as the terminus, because that statement opens up a beautiful vista of dredging to be required in that section-a veritable elysium of dredging. For five or six miles out of Churchill there is a sand bank, and along the banks of the Nelson river for about ten miles dredging would have to be done in order to afford accommodation to vessels. Another advantage in connection with Port Nelson is shown by Mr. Armstrong in his advocacy of the canal system of transportation. I see that the minister has become a convert to that system since his travels in Germany There he found out that the Germans, who are a practical, common-sense people, are in favour of what is after all the democratic way of -conveying freight and passengers-transportation by water; and one of the advantages of Port Nelson, according to Mr. Armstrong's report, is the possibilities of a canal being built, paralleling the railway, down to Fort Nelson and up to Lake Winnipeg. Well, that is not a possibility in the near futnre, 'but it is a possibility, and we may vet have water communication between Winnipeg and Hudson bay. It has that advantage over the Fort Churchill route, because the river is very tumultuous
and precipitous along its course. But I would like to draw the minister's attention to one thing.
