Notwithstanding all the reports and notwithstanding all the references to the particular value of this port or that, through its being a month longer open than any other, the period of navigation is not determined at all by the length of open season at any particular port, but by the navigation of the straits. It does not matter if you have a port open the whole year round, if you can only navigate the straits during four months.
The minister talked about a saving of five cents in the transportation of grain. Well, we had that question discussed ad nauseam some 25 years ago, and the statement was made that we could send grain from Winnipeg and most of the points along the Canadian Pacific railway to the head of Lake Superior cheaper than we could send it to Hudson bay. Calculations were made again and again to prove that from the head of Lake Superior to Liverpool grain could be delivered cheaper than from Fort Churchill to Liverpool. -That may seem strange. There are six months' navigation in Lake Superior and the St. Lawrence. The vessels engaged in that trade sail from Montreal and Quebec to Liverpool and have only seven months navigation. But they have this advantage. The other five months of the year they can be employed in other parts of the world. The steamers for the Hudson Bay route must be specially constructed for that service, and so they will be engaged for four months in the year and be obliged to lie idle for the remaining eight months. However, the scheme looks beautiful and no doubt the government will endeavour to carry it out. But, I mention these things to dispel if possible the idea the minister seems to have that five cents per bushel will be saved on northwest grain by sending it via the Hudson bay. From all the information I was able to gather at that time I believe it to be a practical fact that you can take grain from the western country down to Lake Superior and over to Great Britain cheaper than you possibly can byi the Hudson Bay route. If that be so, and I think it is, the necessity for the Hudson Bay railway is not very pressing. I venture to draw the attention of the government, when the Transcontinental railway was proposed to the House, to the mistake made in the estimated cost of that railway and the minister now tells us that it is estimated that the Hudson Bay railway with its terminals, will cost about $18,000,000. Well, even $18,000,000 is a very large expenditure on top of the other enormous expenditures we are now mqking for the building of railways and the improvement of our means of transportation. Let me tell the minister that

if he studies carefully the question he will find that the solution of the transportation problem in this country is the building of the Georgian Bay canal. I have advocated that project for years. God knows I have no personal interest in it, nor have my constituents because we are situated half way between the two charmers1, the St. Lawrence river and the Ottawa river. It may be affectation for me to mention that I speak from the bottom of my heart when I say that the Georgian Bay canal would be the wisest scheme this government could undertake now. Nature has favoured us by placing us in a position geographically to control not only the trade of Canada but the trade of the northern part of the American continent. I am glad that the minister is converted to a certain extent to my views because he has expressed the sentiment which I have just given utterance to, and when he did so I wondered if he had in his eye the Georgian Bay canal. Let me counsel the government: Be economical in all your expenditures, be economical because the country needs economy and because by practising^ it you will teach the people what is right and wrong in the science of government. I have studied the question from my boyhood upwards, I know the geography of the country, and I ask the government to take my word for it that the solution of the transportation problem is the building of the canal along the route followed by the old voyagers, up the Ottawa, across Lake Nipissing and along the northern shore of Lake Superior to the west. Enough upon that question; we have to deal with a good many questions tonight and-1 would like to be brief.
The Minister of Railways directed our attention to the $7,000,000 already expended on the Quebec bridge, and to my mind nothing has happened in -this country so disgraceful as the action of the government in connection with that particular bridge. We were induced to subscribe a lot of money for the purpose of assisting in building that bridge. The bridge belonged to a company; it was assisted not only by the Dominion government but by the province of Quebec and the city of Quebec. When the bridge tumbled down you would have thought that the contractors and the parties who were interested in the corporation building the bridge would have suffered some loss. But no, out of the generosity of our hearts we paid them all the money the members of this company had advanced and we paid them interest upon .it; we paid back all the money contributed by the city of Quebec and by the province of Quebec to aid in its construction, aryl we took the concern over holus-bolus. That was an act of generosity unparalleled in the history of the world.
Act of generosity; it was more like an act of dishonesty.

I am not saying there is any dishonesty at all about it, It might have been done for state or political reasons. The Prime Minister represents the city of Quebec and he was interested that the city should not suffer, but I do not believe there was anything corrupt about it; if there was I do not know of it nor have I ever heard any authority for it, and I am merely stating the facts I know of. What is the position now? After the bridge fell we employed engineers to devise a scheme for the substructure and the superstructure of the new bridge. The minister tells us to-night that these engineers have agreed upon the plans for the substructure, but they have not yet been able to decide whether it is to be a cantilever or a suspension bridge, and so they will call for tenders for each kind of bridge. And the minister tells us that he will not furnish us with the estimate of the cost. That is curious; it is the first time I ever heard of such a thing in this parliament. When the government comes to parliament for money to build an undertaking the first thing they do is to furnish the plans of the engineers and the estimates of the cost, and then they ask us for the money. But we are told that if that were done in this case it might give an advantage to some contractor. Well, if the minister is in any way afraid of that he could put the estimates pretty low and that would get him out of the difficulty. You remember when the Transcontinental railway was under discussion how the Minister of Finance told us that 'after making a minute calculation and after taking various things into consideration, the whole cost to the country would represent only $13,000,000. I told the minister what I believed would be the cost of the Transcontinental railway, I told him that the cost would be in the neighbourhood of $70,000 per mile from Winnipeg to Moncton, I told him that the statement he made in reference to $13,000,000 would not cover the Quebec bridge alone. We have already lost on that bridge in the neighbourhood of $7,000,000. Will that bridge and the approaches to it ever be completed for less than $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 more? It will cost in the neighbourhood of $15,000,000 to $18,000,000. When the road was under contemplation, I stated that the Quebec bridge alone would cost more than the sum which the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister said would be the cost of the railway; it is turning out to be so now. Let us see what that road is likely to cost. According to the books, the expenditure on the Grand Trunk Pacific up to the end of last year was $53,000,000.
I think the figures I gave this afternoon were $67,000,000.

I am basing my statement on the report, not reckoning to the end of the fiscal year. Now, see what an enormous liability will rest upon the country for the cost of the prairie section, 915 miles from Wolf Creek to Winnipeg. That was to cost $13,000 a mile, and we supplemented that by a loan of $10,000,000. The cost of the prairie section, according to Mr. Schreiber, will be $33,007,449. On the eastern section from Moncton to Winnipeg, 1,804 miles, we have spent, up to March 30 last year, $51,950,000. Mr. Lumsden calculated that it would cost $66,427 per mile, making $114,395,765. The interest during construction-I am supposing it will take seven years to construct-will be about $10,000,000. The interest we will have to pay for seven years after construction will be $14,422,000. The terminals at Moncton, Winnipeg and other places will cost $5,600,-
000.	The Quebec bridge, on which we have already spent $7,000,000, will cost at least $8,000,000 to $10,000,000 more. I calculate that the mountain section of the road will cost about $75,000 per mile for somewhat over 800 miles. We have not got from the chief engineer or from the department any information of the actual cost; I am putting it at $75,000 per mile, so that the interest on the total cost will be $10,000,000. We have now reached a grand total of $167,-
716,000.	Then we advance on the prairie section a loan of $11,895,000. Upon the mountain section we guarantee $75,000 a mile, or $62,700,000. Add to the two latter sums the $10,000,000 loan, and we have $84,595,000 to add to the $167,000,000.
Now there is a possibility that that portion of the road from the Pacific to Winnipeg will be paying in a short while, so that it will not be a charge upon the country. It may be worth what has been expended on it. The prairie section must be supplemented by contributing lines of railway; as at present projected, it cannot become a paying concern unless branch lines are built connecting with it. A single line of railway passing through a prairie can only levy for a certain number of miles north and south of it, and from this source it could not derive revenue enough to keep it running. They will have to build lines of railway paralleling the main line for the purpose of assisting the main line. Now there is a possibility that the line to the head of Lake Superior wil never become a charge on the government of the country. What will the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway company do? The moment they find that the road from Winnipeg to Moncton is not a paying road, are they likely to continue running it? What means have you of forcing them to do so? You may say that you have a lien upon the stock. Well, your lien upon the
stock only becomes valid along with the lien held by the parties who bought the stock. What lien have you upon the road that is being built? You had a lien prior to the company borrowing money for the purpose of constructing that road, and you gave it away to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Your lien at the present time runs pari pagsu with that of the parties who have loaned money on the prairie section and the mountain section; and how are you going to enforce it for the benefit of the eastern section? You may say that they owe you the money. You take the road and you work it and run it. But who do you take it and run it for? You work it and run it for the benefit of yourselves and other creditors who have with you a lien upon the road. What means have you to compel the Grand Trunk Railway company, who you say have entered into an engagement with you, to work the eastern section of the road? Supposing you obtained an order from the court that the Grand Trunk railway must work it, what penalty could be imposed on the Grand Trunk for refusing? The franchise of the Grand Trunk railway lies in the common stock, and the common stock is worth little or nothing. It is only worth something for speculative purposes' I am not going to say a word against the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk has done a great deal for Canada. The men who put their money into the Grand Trunk have not had the results which they expected from that investment. The people of Canada owe a great deal to the Grand Trunk. I am only pointing out the position of the government with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. If they do not work the road from Winnipeg to Quebec to your satisfaction, what are you going to do? Take over the road, the rolling stock and everything else? You take over, as I say, the western section, subject to the lien upon it held by the parties who have advanced money, subject to the claim on the rolling stock and subject to your own lien. You stand pari passu with the parties who advanced the money for the construction of the road. But, you have no tangible claim whatever for the purpose of enabling you to take the road over. The same is true of the eastern section. You say to the Grand Trunk: Go on and work that road. They say: We have spent money enough on the undertaking, we have found out that it is impossible to operate the road from Winnipeg to Moncton with satisfactory results and -we will not run it; run it yourselves. You have no remedy against the Grand Trunk. The only result will be that you will take possession of it. Fancy the government in possession of a Toad on which they have expended $164,000,000 with no connection at Winnipeg and with no connection with Lake Superior, because the key to the situation, the branch line

from Superior Junction to Lake Superior, is in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. They refused to mortgage it or give it as a security for this undertaking. The parties who own the road, own that branch independently, and this government has no claim upon it. You have the road on your hands, you have to work it, and you not only lose the interest on the $164,000,000, but you have the road passing through a country not at all comparable with that which the Intercolonial railway passes through. The result will be that you will operate that road at a cost which will make the people very sick of the undertaking. It would be better for them if you had pitched the whole of the money into the sea rather than that you should have invested it in any such undertaking. There are possibilities. Some mineral discoveries may be made in the country. Some bonanza in the shape of a Cobalt, gold mines, or chance development may give an impetus to the Toad which does not exist at the present time. The wildest scheme that was ever propounded to the people of any country was the idea of drawing grain from Winnipeg over the western section of the road down to Quebec, across the bridge, and from there to St. John and Halifax, and establishing an undertaking in competition with other roads. We all know that the cheapest manner of transporting grain or heavy freight of any kind is by water. President Taft of the United States, in making comparisons, says that transport by water can be carried on at one-eighth of what it costs by rail. I think that perhaps he is too low; at any rate, let us say one-quarter. That is the cheapest way of conveying heavy freight. What is the result? Grain from the west to the markets of the east will seek the quickest possible way, and that is by means of water communication. The large carrying companies realize the importance of water carriage. The Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific railway all go to Fort William to take advantage of water transportation. No all-rail communication can compete with water communication from the head of Lake Superior down to the sea. That is one of the reasons why I am an advocate of the Georgian bay canal. It is the cheapest means of transporting the great products of the west to the sea-board. I have shown the enormous expenditure that this country will have to undertake. It will have to pay interest on $164,000,000 plus the cost of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton for the next thirty or forty years. The Grand Trunk is not going to do it. Any one who looks with a prescient eye ahead must say that the results I predict will come. If no other result comes, see rvhat an enormous burden it places upon us. Why did the government not build the line as laid down and Mr. J. G. HAGGART.
advised by the opposition? The opposition were in favour of opening up the west, they stated their plan and showed how the road ought to be built, but I do not believe that the right hon. gentleman could carry out this scheme with the aid of his supporters, unless he agreed that there should be a summer terminus at Quebec and winter termini at St. John and Halifax. Fancy building a road paralleling the Intercolonial railway, our own road, that does not pay at the present moment. They claim that they are shortening the distance by 120 miles. But, does it shorten it any? Sir Sanford Fleming tried to get a better line for the Intercolonial railway, and if such a line could have been obtained, surely he ought to have known it. For years they have been exploring down there. They have their line practically completed, and what do they find? They find that they cannot get a much better line or any shorter line from Levis to Moncton than the old route of the Intercolonial railway. They at present have a railway that they hardly know what' to do with. The Intercolonial railway is a puzzle to them, and there is a deficit on it from year to year except during the last nine months, with which I intend to deal presently. They have built a harbour at Port Colborne at an expenditure of $3,500,000 which has not fulfilled the expectations of hon. gentlemen opposite. Ships were to go down there that would otherwise go to Buffalo; they were to unload a portion of their cargo at Port Colborne, pass through the canal, and go down the St. Lawrence. I told them at the time that if a vessel wanted to load to go to Montreal or Quebec, it was just as easy for it to go to the port of Buffalo, 10 or 15 miles away and get the cargo from a vessel there, instead of spending $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 for the purpose of building this elevator at Port Colborne. They no sooner had it built than the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), in his tour through the west, promised the people in that section the deepening of the Welland canal. What use .would the elevator at Port Colborne be after the deepening of the Welland canal? You have 21-foot navigation in the port, and you will have 21-foot navigation on the canal. Vessels will not stay in the port at all, they will go clear through the canal. It is a useless expenditure of $4,000,000. The hon. minister does not seem to be pleased with the business done by the elevator, but he hopes that in the future it will develop. It has been built now and running for over a year and actually 1,000,000 bushels have gone into that elevator, one of the largest in the country. It has been an entirely useless expenditure.
Let us come to the question immediately before the House, the management of the Intercolonial railway. The people of this country will hardly believe the amount that

Canada has expended on the Intercolonial railway. I suppose very few of them read the blue-books, but if they look at the report issued by the Minister of Railways this year they will find the extraordinary statement that $91,000,000 has been expended on capital account of the Intercolonial railway, and nearly $8,900,000 on the Prince Edward Island railway, and for the nine months, bringing the figures down to the present day, there has been a further expenditure of $1,200,000 on the Intercolonial railway. From 1896 up to the present moment the capital expenditure on the Intercolonial railway and its branches has increased from $49,000,000 up to the neighbourhood of $102,000,000. What benefit has the country got from it? What is the difference whether you charge an amount to ordinary revenue or to capital account? The minister never thinks of paying the interest on his capital account. He makes comparisons between what is charged to capital account by this railway and other railways, but he forgets that the Baltimore and Ohio and the others with which he makes comparisons pay interest on the capital account. How long suffering have the people of Canada been? From mismanagement-and I shall prove the mismanagement out of the evidence produced by the Minister of Railways this year-the debt on the Intercolonial railway, or the capital account, has increased in fourteen years from $50,000,000 to $102,000,000. The hon. gentleman says: Oh, the great benefit the Intercolonial railway is to the people in that section of the country! I would like to see figures in support of the statements of the Minister of Railways that the intercolonial railway carries freight and passengers for less than any other railway. The passenger rate is the same
I think I stated that the passenger rates were about the same as on other roads, I think they are; the freight rates are cheaper.

I said that the hon. gentleman stated that the passenger rates were the same on the Intercolonial railway as on other roads. He said that the freight rates were greatly below the freight rates on other roads. The freight paid by the ordinary merchant, farmer or other customer along the Intercolonial railway is, I venture to say, as high as on any road in Ontario or Quebec. I looked into the question and I state that the people of the maritime provinces pay a fair price on all the freight they carry. The average is brought down by the rates on two or three commodities. Coal, lumber, shingles and some other things-and the coal is principally carried out of the maritime provinces-are carried at a ridiculously low rate. But as a general rule the freight rates on the Intercolonial railway are on an average about
the same as in other sections of this country. The passenger rates are the same and the freight rates are the same. Then why is it that it costs so much to run the road? Why i3 it that there is deficit after deficit? Last year I drew the attention of the minister to the enormous number of employees on the road, a number largely in excess of its requirements. He evidently found my complaint to be well founded, for he tells us to-day that the Commission of Management, who were appointed to manage the road have discharged about 600 men. Then last year it cost a greater amount to collect the revenues on the Intercolonial than it did the preceeding year. Last year they collected less and paid more. Something wrong about that, $600,000 less collected and it cost a couple of hundred thousand dollars more. It is an anomaly, and the officers ought to be obliged to explain it.
The appointment of a commission to manage the Intercolonial is a peculiar move. Who are the commissioners? The deputy head of the Railway Department, Mr. Pott-inger, the manager o.f the road; Mr. Brady, Mr. Tiffin, all members of the staff of the Intercolonial. The curiosity is that when they are under the direct direction of the Minister of Railways the affair goes to the devil. Joined together, meeting together for the purpose of managing the road, they do first rate.
That is a good idea.

I know Mr. Pottinger, the manager of the road, perfectly well. Give him his instructions and lie will carry them out. It is a difficult thing for the manager of the road, when he knows there are a lot of incapables or old men on the road not fitted for their positions and not able to do their work. He does not like to discharge them-it is human nature. He has a kind heart like the Minister of Railways, who interested himself with the commissioners on behalf of a lot of the employees. Mr. Pottinger is a good and efficient manager of the railroad. Give him his instructions, and he will carry them out. Take him to your office, and say to him: Here are the mistakes and faults in the management of the road; you have too many men; make a comparison of the freight rates on your road and those on other roads-why cannot you manage and give as good results as they can? And he will say:	Give
me a free hand;	get rid of the
political influences that are tempting me or making me do otherwise; let there be no political influence in the management of the road, and I will manage it as economically and as well as any other manager in Canada can. I had occasion to test this matter when I was Minister of Railways. I found a similar state of affairs to -what the hon. gentleman found when

he came into office. I sent for Mr. Pottin-ger and Mr. Schreiber, both capable men. I said to Mr. Pottinger: I want such and such results. It can be done, but you must discharge such a number of men. Is it possible to do it without degrading the character of the road, impairing the rolling stock or lowering the standard below what it is at present? I want the rails, the stations and the rolling stock all kept up; can you do it and give me such results? And he said:	I can if you give me
a free hand. He was given a free hand. He found that he had 1,200 men on the road more than were necessary, placed there through political influences. I am not accusing one political party of being worse than the other in this respect; but the minister can keep control, even with the commission that exists at present, though it may act as a go-between between himself and his political supporters in the House. But if he insists on a satisfactory result, it can be got, and it can be got only from a minister who does not represent the maritime provinces. It is a good selection to take a Minister of Eail-way-s from another province. If he exercises the power and the honesty which I believe' from the bottom of my heart he has, though I differ from him politically,
. he can manage the affairs of that department so that it will be an honour and credit to the country, and there is no man on this side of the House who would not be proud to see him do it. There is no trouble in doing it. It is just as easy to have a million dollars of revenue from the Intercolonial railway, with the freight and passenger rates as they are at present, as to have the present state of affairs. There has been a saving of over $700,000 in the last nine months under the commission. That looks hopeful of a saving of nearly $1,000,000 a year; and $1,500,000 or perhaps $2,000,000 could be saved as easily. When I was Minister of Railways the Intercolonial railway was a little affair. The total receipts and expenditures were in the neighbourhood of $3,000,000 a year. Now the receipts and expenditures are over $9,000,000 a year, which shows that either the population or the business of the maritime provinces during the last fourteen years has wonderfully increased. There is three times the business done now on the Intercolonial railway that there was in 1896. Why is it that every railway of any enterprise in Canada is paying well except the Intercolonial?
Now, let me criticise the statement furnished by the commissioners. The expenditure on capital account for the year will be approximately $1,280,000, against $3,867,232 for the previous year. But the extraordinary thing is that the Prince Edward Island railway, with receipts of Mr. J. G. HAGGART.
about $200,000 and an expenditure of nearly $300,000, had a capital expenditure last year of about $500,000.
Not all on the railway-proper.

It was for enlarged accommodation at stations, sidings and a lot of other things, among them a judgment against the railway obtained by a man who was building a bridge down there. The gross receipts on the Intercolonial for the nine months ending December 31 amounted to $7,073,300, an increase of $442,154 over the corresponding nine months of the previous year. The gross working expenses for the nine months amounted to $6,310,912, a reduction of $757,087. What I want to draw the attention of the minister to is this:	He
collected during the nine months of this year $442,000 more than he did during the same period last year, and yet he expended $750,000 less in that same period. That is an extraordinary statement. You have an increased revenue of $442,000 in the nine months and a decreased expenditure _ of $757,000. There must have been a startling condition of affairs in the preceding year when such a reduction in expenditure and increase in revenue were possible, or there must have been a considerable charging up of ordinary expenditure against capital account. I want to draw the attention of the House to the enormous capital account on the Intercolonial railway. We hope for better days, but we have a deficit now which will amount this year to about $800,000.
A surplus.

No, a deficit. The $1,200,000 charged to capital account ought to be charged to ordinary expenditure, and I so stated w-hen that amount was voted for particular expenditures. You can never have an honest statement from the officials of any railway when they have the right to manipulate their capital account just as they please. There ought to be no such thing as a capital account in a railway belonging to a government. It is not an account on which we expect any interest to be paid, and consequently should be wiped out altogether. In saying this I am not merely expressing my own opinion, but I am repeating the statement made again and again by the right hon. gentleman who leads the House when he used to attack the late Sir John Macdonald and the Conservative party for having a capital account on the Intercolonial railway and concealing extravagant expenditures under that head. The right hon. gentleman said: You can have no honest, no trustworthy management of the Intercolonial or any other government enterprise until the cap-

ital account is wiped out altogether. So it should be because there is no need for it. There would not be any such capital account in any other country in the world. We charge a lot of expenditure in this country to capital which is not done in other countries. When we build fortifications, we charge them to capital account as well as a lot of expenditure from one end of the country to the other. Just fancy a Dreadnought being built by the British government and charged to capital account or a dock at Malta or Gibraltar. There is no such thingt as capital account in the British public accounts, and there ought to be none here. Let us have a plain statement of the expenditure on the road and let us form our own conclusions as to whether that expenditure was judicious or not. The minister has no basis for making a comparison between the Intercolonial and company owned railways in this connection. The directors of railway companies have to provide an income out of which to pay interest on the capital, but there is no interest paid on the Intercolonial and never will be. I am hoping for better tilings. There has been a little better management than in the past. I believe the hon. gentleman is trying to do something. Let him bend all his energy to obtaining an honest administration of his department, either by a commission or something else. I have no faith myself in commissions, and the hon. gentleman had very little when he appointed this one. The suggestion came from my leader (Mr. Borden), who drew a comparison between the Intercolonial railway and the government railways in Australia and other places, which are managed by commissions and gave good results. He thought that the government railway in this country might be managed by a commission with like good results. Of course we know that the * people of the maritime provinces will not allow what they consider a peculiarly maritime interest to be owned by. any railway company, but some other method of management might be devised. It might be run in the interests of the three railwav companies which connect with it. Or there might be a joint stock arrangement, in which the three different railways interested would pool, each its share" of the earnings, and share each the cost of the management. I thought, that perhaps something of that kind might be possible, but we should always have a string to that railway. Should Lloyd George's theories prevail in the old country, should the theory of my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) on municipal or state ownership of railways and other public utilities take root in this country, it is possible that the day may come when we might take a new departure along those lines. Let us
then keep control of something we own, and if we should part with the management ourselves, let us always have a string to bring it back to the people. I hope for better things in the future. I see a bright future because the maritime provinces are progressing wonderfully. They are progressing more than the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec, if we can judge by the amount of freight and passengers carried on the different lines in the provinces by the sea. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick particularly are doing three times the business they formerly did. May that business continue to flourish is the wish of every one on this side no matter to what portion of the Dominion he may belong. That these little provinces down by the sea-that portion of the Dominion of which we are so proud-may prosper and flourish and that the peopled railway may be a success is what none desire more ardently than hon. gentlemen on this side.

Before proceeding with the few observations I have to make on the subject under discussion, let me congratulate the hon. minister (Mr. Graham) on the most admirable statement he has given us this afternoon. And let me also felicitate my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Haggart) on the kindly manner of his criticism and, let me assure him that we deeply appreciate the generous sentiments he has uttered and which are all the more welcome, coming from so old a parliamentarian, one whom we mav call the father of the House. I would like at the outset to express the hope that now, when we are about to rebuild the Quebec bridge, the government may see its way to put its construction .in the hands of some of our Canadian bridge builders and artisans. If it be possible to find among them men able to construct that work, the government should take every opportunity to give them the preference and entrust to them this great national undertaking. If they should do this, I am sure that there will be much greater satisfaction among our own people than if they entrusted this enterprise to outsiders. Might I also be permitted to remark that while we hear great solicitude expressed by hon. members from all parts of the country regarding the Intercolonial railway, yet in the maritime provinces where we have to use that railway, we may be admitted to have a greater personal interest in its successful operation than can possibly be felt by hon. gentlemen from other sections.
May I be permitted to say that I do not think that the fact that the Minister of Railways was able to announce a surplus this afternoon is any special reason for

congratulation. I do not know whether my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) who is the apostle of public operation in this country believes that it is the duty of a government which is operating a public utility to milk it to the greatest possible extent. If he does, then I am afraid the admiration for public ownership in any portion of the country that had practical experience of it would speedily fade away. There is one thing about this question which most hon. gentlemen forget, and that is that while it is a most desirable thing to make both ends meet, yet, this year when you have a surplus of $600,000 or $700,000 that surplus becomes of no value to the future of that enterprise. It is not like the balance in the profit and loss account of a company operating a railroad, because under the book-keeping system of the government, when there is a surplus at the end of the financial year that money goes into the^ general revenue of the country, ceases to be available for any purpose whatever in connection with the operation of the road. Hon. gentlemen opposite sometimes complain that expenditures are made on capital account, while on the other hand they insist that the Intercolonial railway should have a surplus. But, the moment a surplus is obtained it is appropriated out of the resources for operating the road and disappears altogether as a factor in the management of that railway. Howr are you going to provide for capital expenditure? how are you going to provide for these accretions which necessarily must be made to any great public work, unless you resort to capital expenditure? I, therefore, say that the fact that we have a surplus of $600,000 or $700,000 this year has no significance from the standpoint of government operation of railways. If for instance this year you have not done as much track repairing as you might have done if you did not put in as many ties as you might have put in, if as much ballasting was not done this year as the year before, it simply means that next year you will have to provide for what you failed to do this year, and when you come to provide for it instead of having the surplus in the treasury as a company would have, your surplus from the year before has disappeared. If, for instance, there should be a falling off in passengers and freight, where is the government going to get the money to make up the deficit. There will be a deficit, the surplus of the preceding year will have vanished from the transactions of the Intercolonial railway, and those gentlemen who have such great solicitude for the Intercolonial railway, but who never travel over it and know nothing about it, will hold up their hands in holy horror. It seems to me that instead of having large surpluses it would be much better if the country would begin to realize Mr. E. M. MACDONALD.
what is the real position of affairs in regard to the public operation of this public utility. It seems to me it would be much better that you should endeavour to provide for the running of your railway, to make both ends meet each year, and to operate it in such a way that deficits would not occur. Referring again to my hon. friend from York (Mr. Maclean) and his pet theories, I would like to know from him whether or not this beautiful system of government operation or government ownership of public utilities that he advocates, means that in the operating of the utility there is to ' be any advantage to the people who are living in the community where the utility is operated?

I will answer my hon. friend in a moment-public ownership means absolutely giving service to the people and not realizing profit on capital, and public ownership is to be judged by the service it gives and nothing else.
At better rates?
At better rates, and public ownership will give a better service and better rates if it is efficiently administered, but there must be efficiency of administration.

And my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) holds up Germany as an example of public ownership, and yet Germany took out of the people rates sufficient to pay six per cent on capital, and in addition to that a certain stated amount every year.
And under public ownership in Germany they have the best express service in the world.
But not the best freight service.
Yes, I will tell you about the freight service later on.

I should have known that if my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) got started on his pet theory I would never be able to get a look in at all, and now I hope to be permitted to com tinue my remarks. What I desired to know from my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) was whether one of his theories that the people who were to be served by the utility should have the advantage of better rates than if the utility were operated by a private company. If I underestand my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) aright that is his idea. But some of his friends are fond of complaining that lower rates of freight are obtainable on this public utility, the Intercolonial railway, and, therefore, I am at a loss to understand the position of some gentlemen from this larger province who

are such strong apostles of public ownership, but who at the same time are always wanting the Minister of Railways of the day to extract a surplus out of this public utility. It seems to me that when we come to discuss the Intercolonial in this House we forget a good many things. The people of the maritime provinces, at all events those of them whom I represent, are not asking for any exceptional consideration that is not extended to any other portion of Canada, but surely we ought to remember that the Intercolonial railway was constructed for the purpose of promoting trade between the maritime provinces and central Canada. When Canada stretched out towards the Pacific and absorbed the western provinces, Canada pledged her treasury and her public lands for the purpose of providing an interprovincial railway which would reach to the Pacific coast. Canada spent more money on that railway, and it is spending more money from year to year in providing interprovincial communication between the western provinces, than ever Canada dreamt of spending, even comparatively speaking, in the maritime provinces. Therefore, this question should not be regarded in any sectional way, nor should it be considered that those of us who live in the maritime provinces are asking for sectional consideration. We are asking for nothing of the sort. In this connection, let me tell some of these hon. gentlemen some reasons why the Intercolonial does not pay. If a private company were operating the Intercolonial railway to the port of Halifax, whence immigrants come from all countries in Europe, you would have agents of that railway soliciting these people to travel over the Intercolonial railway when they reached Canada. But, is the Intercolonial railway doing that? Is there a single attempt made by passenger agents of the Intercolonial on the continent of Europe or the British isles to sell a single ticket to an immigrant coming to Canada? No. Every other railway is doing it, but yet this Intercolonial railway, which controls the front door of this Dominion for six months in the year through a port which is open all the year around for the arrival of passengers, does not attempt to induce a single emigrant leaving for Canada to utilize that railway. Now, I do not blame the Intercolonial for not doing that; the fault lies ill the inherent difficulty in the operation bWythe government of public utilities which toy hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) is so fond of advocating.

Let me tell my hon. friend that Switzerland has its agents in America soliciting passengers for the state-owned roads in Switzerland, and there 91
is an answer to his question. What Switzerland does could be done by Canada if we believed in the principle.
My hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) is unfortunately not able to speak for all of the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
I do not profess to.

If a proposition had been made to this House at any time to appoint agents of the Intercolonial railway in Europe, we would have a loud wail from hon. gentlemen opposite about the extravagance of spending money in Europe on account of the Intercolonial railway. What is the result? The result is that the Canadian Bacific railway takes practically every immigrant that comes into this country from the east. It takes him at St. John and runs him to Montreal and other points west. If they arrive at Halifax, it brings them to St. John over the Intercolonial, and then they get the long haul on the through ticket to all points in the west. That is one point that hon. gentlemen forget in discussing the Intercolonial. Look at the immigration that is coming into Canada. Every week thousands of people have been coming in during the winter time, landing at our seaports, but the Intercolonial does not get any advantage from them. That is one of the reasons why the Intercolonial does not pay. But there is another reason. If a company were in the position in which the government of this country is in at present, they would long ago have imposed upon goods coming from the mother country under the preference, a restriction that they must come into Canada through Canadian ports. So during particularly six months of the year when these goods come to Canada, the railway would have the opportunity to haul them from the eastern ports under that restriction. But that is not done. The fact is that the Canadian Pacific has the full advantage of that preference in hauling the goods. The Grand Trunk runs from Montreal to Portland, and the goods that come to Portland during the winter under the preference, are brought to Montreal by the Grand Trunk, the Intercolonial gets no advantage from them. Yet hon. gentlemen who want this road to show a surplus, who want it crippled by dismissing its employees, will stand up in this House, as I have heard them in the' last parliament, and object to the proposition that there should be put in force a restriction that the preference should only apply to goods which come in through Canadian ports.
Then look at another difficulty. This railway was originally constructed as an interprovincial railway and it stopped at Riviere



du Loup. But as the march of commerce proceeded towards the west it was extended. Consider in what an isolated position were the whole of the maritime provinces when that railway terminated at Riviere du Loup. So hon. gentlemen opposite purchased a piece of railway, and purchased the St. Charles branch in addition, and extended the Intercolonial railway to Levis, joining it with the Grand Trunk at Chaudiere. Still every part of the maritime provinces was 400 or 500 miles away from the great metropolis of Canada, it had no connection with Ontario, it had no connection with the west, and it was handicapped to a degree that hon. gentlemen can hardly imagine. Where would we have been to-day if this government had not in 1897, purchased the Drummond County railway'and extended it to Montreal? It purchased these two pieces of railway, involving a capital expenditure which helped to increase if to the large figure which the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has spoken of. Yet with even all these expenditures, and with the extension of the Intercolonial railway to Montreal, that road is not to-day a transcontinental line, it is solely a local line. Why? I suppose that there has been no industry in late years that has attracted so much attention as has the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and along with it the Nova Scotia Steel Company, in which a great many people in this part of Canada are interested. These two large industries manufacture in different lines probably more iron and steel products than all the other iron and steel industries of Canada put together. Yet for nearly six months of the year only a small portion of the product of either of these industries passed beyond the city of Montreal. This country imposes upon these products a tax which interfers with their competing in Ontario and points west with products from the United States. When hon. gentlemen complain about the low rates, let me say that while I agree with the minister that in certain schedules the rates are lower for short hauls than they are on company roads, yet in the .majority of the schedules the rates for one hundred miles haul and over are as great and when you come to make a comparison in regard to long hauls, the Intercolonial railway charges just as much as do the company roads in this country. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite wish to continue this impost upon our industries in the maritime provinces. We in Nova Scotia are the only people who produce coal east of the Rocky Mountains, but we cannot send a pound of coal west of the city of Montreal and compete with the Americans. Hon. gentlemen talk about Canada for Canadians, about protecting home industries and all that Mr. E. M. MACDONALD.
kind of thing, and they want the people of the maritime provinces to be screwed down so that the Intercolonial railway may show a surplus. These are things that ought not to be forgotten in discussing a question of this kind, these are some of the difficulties under which we labour.
But there is another thing. Talk about the advantage of the Intercolonial railway! What would my hon. friends think if the Minister of Railways were to come down with a proposition empowering him to develop industries along the line of the Intercolonial railway? All the other big companies do it. Everybody recognizes that that is one of the advantages of company ownership and operation, that companies are able, by virtue of the facility with which the directors can deal with problems of that kind, to develop natural industries along the line of their railway. The Intercolonial railway cannot do that. So I say that hon. gentlemen opposite do not appreciate the difficulties under which we labour, and which I have indicated. Every session hon. gentlemen hold up their hands in horror because my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has not extracted a surplus from the people who use that railway. If he had extracted a surplus, it could only be by injuring and crippling that railroad for the future. I say that for these reasons the minister has no right to have a surplus of $700,000. All that this country has a right to expect of him, seeing that this road was a special feature of confederation, is that he should make both ends meet, and that the interest of the people who live along that line of railway should have his first consideration. You talk about this being a road in which everybody in Canada is interested; of course it is. But, what would my hon. friends from the further west say if we were to criticise railway development and railway problems up there? They would tell us that they ought to have the first say about their own railways.
Now, I do not think every one was satisfied to hear my hon. friend assure the House that he had not interfered with these gentlemen who compose the Board of Management of the Intercolonial. Down in our country we learned long ago, perhaps before some hon. gentlemen in other parts of Canada did, the advantages of responsible government; and the people expect that when you have a minister of the Crovrn entrusted with the the operation of a great public utility, he must be held responsible therefpr. And my hon. friend is responsible for it, and I do not think that he is assuming his full responsibility unless he intimates to this Board of Management what hi3 ideas are as to how they should act. In a free country like this it is impossible to get rid

of ministerial or governmental responsibility. My hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) tells us that he thinks he is getting on all right, but unfortunately for the minister, in the constituency from which I come and in the constituencies of other hon. gentlemen along the line of the Intercolonial railroad, it will not do for us to say that the minister never spoke to these commissioners, because they have learned the lesson of responsibility, they know that the representatives of the people and the government are responsible at all times for the proper carrying out of this public utility, and that they have the right to interfere in the best interests of the people. 'I know the motives that animate my hon. friend in dealing with these matters in that way, but it will not in the slightest degree protect him from the attacks of hon. gentlemen opposite for him to say that he has nothing to do with this Board of Commissioners. I think the minister has the right to interfere with the Board of Management. He has the right to direct the policy of the board, he has the right to say, when they undertake to infringe upon the rights of the people, that these rights must be respected.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) intimates that the way to fix the Intercolonial is to dismiss a great army of people. I think that the action of this board, where they dismissed 503 employees and where, I am free to say, they exercised their judgment to the fullest extent that my hon. friend from Lanark could have wished, was not justified by the circumstances. I think that they could have worked out just the same results without making these dismissals. As a matter of fact the lure of the west is calling from our eastern provinces numerous men and they are going to the railways of the west and of central Canada. Hundreds of men every year are going west and it would not have taken very long to have reduced the staff of the Intercolonial railway without dismissing these men. It must be remembered that in 1908 the Intercolonial railway began to feel the effect of the bad times which the great central railways had endured for the two previous years. Every one knows of the lack of prosperity that existed on the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific railway in 1908. We began to feel that down there and my hon. friend's board, dealing with this question, summarily dismissed these men. I have no objection to the greatest possible economy being exercised in the operation of the road." I quite agree that there have been abuses in the past- abuses that have come down from the time when my hon. friend the member for Lanark was Minister of Railways and Canals. While he endeavoured in his own way to check the demands that were being made 91*
upon him by his political friends in the maritime provinces, he left a condition of affairs that fortunately is gradually disappearing. And, there is no representative of the people of the maritime provinces who would not stand by the minister in every effort he would make to apply the principles of economy to the management of the road by getting rid of unnecessary officials, and so operating the road that the people of the country will have the best service and under conditions where they will be able to do the business in the best possible way.
It will not do to point to some local rates, as the hon. member for Kings-Albert (Mr. McAllister) did the other day. The Intercolonial railway was not built for the purpose of giving a man a local rate on this or that little product to he carried 15 or 20 miles; it was built as a great Canadian enterprise to connect the different provinces of the Dominion together, and the service which it ought to render to this country is that it should break down the barriers which lie between the provinces of the east and the provinces of the west, so that the products of the east may go to the west and the products of the west may be carried to the east. That is what the country expected when it constructed this" road, and that is what it ought to get no matter who directs or controls the road. Unfortunately, this problem of the Intercolonial railway which has been so much discussed in this House, comes back to this difficulty to-day that it is purely a local line. We do not share in the great transportation development of the west, in the great prosperity that has come to Saskatchewan and Alberta, with their influx of population, with their increase in grain production and with all the great accretions which have come to this country. The great product of the west is brought down, as far as transportation goes, over the great trunk systems until it reaches the city of Montreal. A little bit of that pro-duct trickles down to Nova Scotia and the seaports of Canada, but the great proportion of it switches off at Montreal and goes down to Boston, Portland and other American cities. We only ask that this Intercolonial railway should be regarded as a national work, and that it should be so utilized, either by absorption with the great transcontinental railways or otherwise, that every paft of Canada shall share in the development which has come of late years to the western portion of our country. My hon. friend from Lanark need not think that our people 'by the sea are so wedded to the theory of this railway that we would forego absolutely whatever rights we may have to prevent parliament from making it part of the Transcontinental lines. This rail-

way belongs to the Dominion of Canada, it is owned by the people and apparently it cannot be alienated, But what is this country going to do when the Grand Trunk Pacific comes to Moncton? Inside of two years it will be in operation there. Are you going to let the Grand Trunk Pacific go down to the sea? If you are you must utilize the Intercolonial railway or build a new line to reach the seaports. If the Grand Trunk railway goes there, why should not the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern go there, and why should not the Intercolonial railway be utilized so that in our maritime part of the Dominion we should have centred the national termini of the great transcontinental railways? We would have a oneness and connection that we could not get otherwise. We are apt to regard this question upon narrow lines, to look at it from a contracted view point. We would like the Minister of Railways to exercise his full responsibility and to realize that he must be responsible to the people if he is to act in the best interests not only of the maritime provinces, but of the whole of Canada. Let the whole Dominion of Ganada realize that a miserable surplus of a few hundred thousand dollars is no advantage compared with the development of trade routes throughout this country, and if by absorption or connection with other lines the whole of the Dominion can be rounded out as far as trade is concerned in connection with the three great transcontinental lines, you will be doing something which will not only be for the good of Canada, tout will to a great degree obliterate these little local distinctions and local discussions which now characterize the consideration of this question.
I have had repeated occasions to speak to the minister in regard to the method of dealing with claims made to the Railway Department from people living along the line of the Intercolonial for damages by fire, accidents to animals and injuries in various other ways. I say to the minister in all frankness and kindliness, and I know that he will appreciate my attitude in that regard, that this part of his administration of the Intercolonial calls for some remedy. It is a difficulty that has always existed in the past, but if there are advantages in government operation, as the hon. member for York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) thinks there is, I wish to tell him that there is one phase of government operation which presses very hardly upon the good people who live along the line of this public utility, and that is the recovery of damages in such cases as I have spoken of. A few years ago a statute was passed providing that if a man's property is destroyed by fire from a railway, the company is prima facie Mr. B. M. MACDONALD.
liable, the onus is thrown on the company to show that it is not liable, and claims of that kind can be easily settled in a court of law. I ventured to introduce a Bill and it was carried through parliament, which attempted to apply to the government railway the same extent of liability as other railways, but somehow the claims department of the Intercolonial railway has never discovered this on the statutes, and so far as I have been able to discover since that time, although not only in my own constituency but all along the Intercolonial railway, fires have occurred and the liability prima facie existed under the statute, some one connected with the department or somewhere else solemnly undertook to judge the liability and the evidence and the law and decided that the railway was not negligent. While that is a small matter it causes great difficulty and dissatisfaction to people living along the Intercolonial railway. A rule has been put in force of late that when an investigation is held in regard to the merits of a claim the parties having a claim cannot employ a solicitor to come and see that the claim is properly presented. While we have great public questions to deal with, while I have myself ventured to suggest that we should look at this whole problem from a broad view point, here is a matter of detail by satisfactorily adjusting which the minister will render himself and his management very popular along the line of the Intercolonial railway.
I have been for four weeks trying to work out something along that line, and if I am successful, as I think I will be, my hon. friend will be perfectly satisfied.

It is satisfactory to find that my hon. friend is responding so quickly to my suggestion of improvement in this regard. I am sure we will appreciate it. If my hon. friend will realize that it is his duty to tell these commissioners once in a while what they should do and what they should not do, and that he would be really deserving of condemnation instead of praise if he failed to do that, and if he will also realize the importance of the difficulties I have pointed out, and if he does not make the surplus too large next year, I think the whole House will be satisfied because the hen. member for Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart) was especially satisfied to-night.

MADDIN (Cape Breton South.) Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great pleasure of the annual philippic of the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals in bringing down his statement of the report of the board of management of the

Intercolonial railway. I shall deal with but a few of the points in that address. Until a few years ago, up to the time of my election to represent the county of Cape Breton, we enjoyed on the eastern end of the island of Cape Breton, two trains per day from the capital of Cape Breton to the capital of the province, we had what we called the express and the fast express or flier. Within the last four years during the winter months the fast express was taken off the Halifax-Sydney route and a great deal of agitation took place in the eastern part of the province. It was a matter which affected not only the county of Cape Breton but all the counties from Sydney to Halifax, and it also affected the people of the whole province as well as the people of the upper provinces with regard to mail matter and travel. A great deal of agitation was started with a view to having this train put back on the road and one year ago last month on coming up to the House of Commons here, I spoke to the Minister of Railways in the hope that as there was a pronouncement made at that time that even during the summer months a second train would not be put on the Intercolonial railway from Sydney to Halifax, some arrangement might be made for the benefit of the people in the province of Nova Scotia. There was a freight train leaving the city of Sydney at about six o'clock in the evening which was due at Fort Tupper on the Intercolonial railway somewhere about 11 or 12 o'clock at night. An express train left the town of New Glasgow every morning at about 7 o'clock for Halifax, and I suggested to the minister that a sleeping car should be attached to this freight train which would run on schedule to Point Tupper and that one of the numerous freights between Point Tupper and New Glasgow should be run on schedule to connect with the expiess from New Glasgow to Halifax. The Minister of Railways stated to me at that time that it was his intention to make some change in connection with the Intercolonial railway, and that as this change would be taking place very shortly he did not deem it wise to put on another train or make any alteration in connection with the administration of the affairs of the road. Some time subsequent to this the new board of railway management and control was appointed. I called on one of the members of the board and submitted the proposition to him. He said that in all probability the proper thing would be to have a regular express train. He said to me: Mr. Maddin that end of the road does not pay. Here I would like to recall a question which 1 asked the Minister of Railways on the 5th of May, last:

1. Wliat were the earnings from freight shipped from the Island of Cape Breton over the Intercolonial railway in 1908?
2. What were the earnings from freight shipped to the Island of Cape Breton over the Intercolonial railway in 1908?
3.	What was the revenue from the sale of passenger tickets to passengers going to and coming from the Island of Cape Breton for the year 1908, on the said railway?

1.	Separate accounts iare not kept for this portion of the Intercolonial railway.
2.	Answered by number one.
3.	Answered by number one.
I was told by the board of control that this end of the railway did not pay, and that consequently it was not desirable that another train should be put on lov the convenience of the public. I submit that until the Minister of Railways adopts a system of book-keeping which will show what the earning capacity of the eastern end. of the Intercolonial is, he is not in a position to tell us that the road does not pay. In discussing the freight earnings of the eastern end *of the road with this member of the board of control, I forget whether it was Mr. Butler or Mr. Brady, I pointed out the enormous freights carried for the Nova Scotia Steel Company and the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. That gentleman told me that these freights were hauled at practically a loss-that there was a very heavy grade at George's river, and that in order to haul heavy trains over that grade, it was necessary to cut them up into short trains, so that the freight could not he hauled profitably at the rates charged to those industries. He also said, what was quite proper, that it was not the policy of the Intercolonial to increase the rates for moving steel billets from those works, in view of the fact that they received bounties fr'em the government, and it would not be right for the federal treasury to pay bounties for the production of steel and take them away by charging high rates of freight on the product. That is a view which I think all members of this House will readily agree with. But just before this government went to the country in 1908, a pledge was given to the people of Cape Breton that the grades at George's river would be reduced, and the sum of $350,000, if I remember rightly, was placed in the estimates for that purpose. During the passage of the estimates last session, I pointed out to the Minister of Railways and Canals that there was in the estimates a sum of only $50,000, which he said was there for the purpose of purchasing a right of way for the proposed reduction of grades, and owing to the depression of trade in the country he did not deem it expedient to place a sum in the estimates last year for

the work. But in view of the fact that the Minister of Railways and Canals has assured this House that in the supplementary estimates to be brought down at a subsequent date, the sum of $16,000,000 will be placed for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, and in view of the further fact that a surplus of $666,388.67 has been declared for a period of nine months operation of the Intercolonial railway, a surplus which the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) said the minister should not have declared, it is due to the people at the eastern end of the Intercolonial that a sum be placed in the supplementary estimates for the completion of the promised survey and reduction of grades at George's river in the county of Cape Breton; and I -wish to ask the Minister of' Railways and Canals now if it is his intention to place in the supplementary estimates a sum to be applied for that purpose?
speakername: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals):

speechtext: Is there not a sum for it' in the main estimates?
No.
Look again, my hon. friend must be mistaken.

Last year the estimated cost of the reduction of the grade, as given to us by the Minister of Railways and Canals, was a sum exceeding $400,000. I took the ground then that the sum of $50,000 was not adequate. I was told that it was placed there only for the purpose of purchasing the right of way, and that it was not proposed to take any active steps in connection with the matter. In the estimates for this year there is the sum of $100,000; but in view of the statement of the minister that $400,000 will be required, that sum is not adequate for the carrying on of this work, and I ask the minister if it is intended to place a sum in the supplementary estimates sufficient for the carrying out of this work?
The work cannot all be done in one season. We are doing with this work what we are doing with every work, placing in the estimates an adequate amount for the work to be done this season.
What work was done for the $50,000 which was in the estimates last year?
There was considerable work done.

Well, it seems to me that the Department of Railways and Canals are not exhibiting the same anxiety for the reduction of grades at George's river in the years 1009 and 1910 that they exhibited in 1908, before the elections. In answer to a question put last session, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals said that the engineer had gone down to make the surveys Mr. MADDIN.
for the reduction of these grades as promptly as he could after the House closed. Although he hastened down and made the surveys after the House closed in 1908, there has been no actual work done there from that time to the present.
Now, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has told us with some assurance that there has been no interference from him with the administration of the railway under the board of control. I admire the courage of the hon. member for Pictou, who took the minister to task and told him what his responsibilities in connection with the administration of that railway really are. If the hon. member for Pictou demonstrated anything this evening, it was that he, and not the present incumbent of that portfolio, should be administering the railway in the maritime provinces. I doubt if any hon. member on either side of the House has much ground to complain of interference on the part of the Minister of Railways,' either the present incumbent of that office or any of his predecessors. I think the railway has suffered much more from the lack of interference- than from interference on the part of the minister. Last year, when the Railway Board was appointed, we were given the strongest assurance through the Liberal press of the country that the railway was now brought out of the range of politics, and that from now, henceforth and for ever, there would be no interference from politicians with the administration of the affairs of the road. People imagined that this was actually the fact, for it was only a short time after the appointment of the new board that 503 heads fell into the basket, the result of the over-manning of the road during the general elections in the fall of 1908. While the Minister of Railways plumes himself on not having interfered with the road, I think it would be much more to the credit of himself and his administration if he could have assured us that there had been no interference with the affairs of the road by men of lesser responsibility than himself.
I wish to point out that in the month of June last, when these 503 men were dismissed, a gentleman by the name of James Edwards, a boilermaker in Sydney, was suspended in the mechanical department at that end of the road. He was told by the foreman that he need not take his tool box away, that he was not dismissed but merely suspended, and that if an opening should occur in that line of work, his serviced would be required again. But permit me? to diverge for a moment to "something that took place previous to this. In the fall of 1908, about a week before the general elec-1 t.ions in Cape Breton, Mr. Edwards, the boilermaker, was sent for by Alexander Johnson, the Liberal candidate in Cape Breton South, and was invited by him to

the office of the * Daily Record.' On entering Mr. Johnson's presence, he was addressed as follows:
So you are the man who was cheering for Maddin out in ward 4. You ought to take a tumble to yourself. See if Maddin can get you a job.
This was in the fall of 1908. In June, 1909, this man was suspended along with others. But his tool box remained in the shop, and he was told that when a vacancy occurred and his services would be required he would be sent for. Being aware that there was a vacancy, he went down and sought for re-employment, but his employer said to him: You will have,do make your peace with the Liberal party. Edwards said:	I thought the commissioners said
there was to be no politics or seniority on the Intercolonial. His boss replied: Do you think if I wanted to hire ten mechanics I could go and hire ten of the best men to be found regardless of their politics? No, I would have to go to Mr. Johnson or Dr. Kendall for every one of them. Mr. Edwards then called on Dr. Kendall, the local member, and complained of unfair treatment, and the doctor promised to make inquiries. He met the doctor on the street a couple of days afterwards, and the doctor said to him: Edwards, I understand how it is about your job. You were working for Maddin against Mr. Johnson. See if Mr. Maddin can get you a job. Edwards said: I thought politics and seniority had nothing to do with the railway, that it would be run on a new principle, _ independent of politics. He said: We will let you see that. And Edwards is still unemployed. If the road were purged of the_ administration of its affairs by politicians and ex-politicians, those who have graduated from this House, and are taking a post graduate course in journalism and provincial politics-if this road were purged of the operations of these ex-politicians, and a little more attention paid by the Minister of Railways, who is really the one responsible for its administration, there would be fewer complaints.
Something has been said with regard to the Hudson Bay railway, and we are, given to understand that this railway is to be taken up by the government and completed. Well, we have had reports to the effect that there is only navigation in that bay for some two months in the year and that in the straits there is navigation for less than two months. As every one is aware, the class of vessel required to go through the drifting ice are vessels of slow speed, high power, sheathed in wood to resist the ice jam. These vessels have to be specially constructed and are unfit for other traffic. If this railway is completed and is going to remove the crop of the west, it will only defer the building of the Georgian
Bay canal. The hou. member for Pictou has pointed out that we are only able to ship our coal from the province of Nova Scotia up to Montreal, and cannot ship it beyond that point. But if the Georgian Bay canal were completed, I submit that coal could be shipped from Cape Breton to Port Arthur as cheaply, if not cheaper than it can be landed at Montreal to-day. A great drawback with regard to getting coal into the upper Canadian market is the question of transportation. The vessels built for carrying coal to Montreal are obliged to come back in water ballast, but if the Georgian Bay canal were built they would carry coal to Port Arthur and get return freight so that coal could be landed at Port Arthur as cheaply, if not cheaper, than at Montreal at present. But if this government is going to experiment in millions of dollars expenditure on the Hudson Bay railway, in order to have shipments for a couple of months, that will only delay the construction of the Georgian Bay canal.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) said that my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) was opposed to the government rates charged on the Intercolonial railway on traffic coming east or going west. I would like to point out that the hon. gentleman was not complaining about the dearness' of the rate, but what he did complain of was that the railway did not pay, although there was no reason why, with the passenger and freight rates that were being charged it should not.
In his address to the House this afternoon, the Minister of Railways dealt with the different canal projects and western railway and finally wound up with a report of the Intercolonial. He went into the expenditure and revenue of this road and took a good deal of time to point out that this year in particular, there was a surplus, instead of a deficit. I submit that there should not be exhibited this undue anxiety on the part of the minister in his annual presentation, because the Intercolonial railway was never intended to be a revenue earning railway. The hon. minister has told us that he has great faith in the future of this country. He believes that in the course of the next twenty-five years all the great public works now projected will be completed and that even then we will not have more highway than we require for our freight and passengers. Let me tell him that the Intercolonial railway was projected and built at a period of our history when' it required more faith than is required to-day to foresee the benefits bound to arise to this country from its construction. In the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, men were not lacking before confederation who would undertake to build the Intercolonial railway as far as Riviere du Loup. It was not built for the

purpose of earning revenue, but for the purpose of developing the resources of our country down by the sea. It was constructed for the purpose of carrying products of the mines, the forests, the fisheries and the farms to the different markets of the world and to bring in to those provinces the imports required for their development and maintenance.
It was assumed by those who brought this railway into existence that it possibly might be run at a loss; it certainly never was expected that it would be made a revenue paying concern. Let me ask if the Minister of Railways exhibits any very great anxiety year after year because the canals in Upper Canada, which cost the country over $100,000,000, and through which the people of Nova Scotia cannot ship a single ton of coal, are not paying dividends, and yet we all know that the canals were made free and that they were rot even expected to pay their way. This $100,000,000 expenditure of canals is practically of no use to the people of the maritime provinces, but do we raise an annual vail because the canals don't pay? No. We realize that our canal system in Upper Canada is necessary to the development of that part of the Dominion, and might we not with some reason be allowed to hope that the railway system in the maritime provinces should be looked upon in somewhat the same light. The Intercolonial railway is to some extent looked upon by the people of the maritime provinces as more particularly an asset of these provinces, just as the canals may be looked upon as an asset of the1 people of western Canada. Do we hear the members from the maritime provinces complaining about the employment of too many men on the canals or the dismissal of men on the canals? Oh, no, but year after year the government is asked: Are they going to sell the Intercolonial, or are they going to lease it, or are they going to put it under a Royal Commission, or are they going to get rid of the incubus in some way. I submit. Sir, that if the Intercolonial were freed from political influences which yet characterize its management there would be less complaint about it.
