I shall not draw any comparison between the administration under Conservative rule and under Liberal rule, I am not going to say that political influence did not exist in the days of the Conservative administration, but we all know it is a recognized fact that at the present time political influence is exercised in connection with everything appertaining to the Intercolonial, from the hiring of a common labourer to buying of stores and the making of contracts. It was recognized 'that patronage and partyism permeated the management of the l'oa'd throughout, and when the board of management was

appointed we were promised that these influences would be got rid of. But let me say, Sir, that so far from this board being now free from external political influences that is not the case, and in that respect their administration has been a failure. Now, coming more particularly to details, I trust the minister will see that the grades on the Intercolonial railway at George's river will be reduced immediately. The minister has now a surplus which is more than sufficient to pay for this work, and the excuse that he made a year ago that the financial conditions of the country do not warrant the expenditure has now disappeared. I trust he will in the near future carry to completion the reduction of the grades at George's river, which will be a great improvement to the system.

Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee of Supply.
Railways and canals-capital-Intercolonial Railway-Beresford subway, $6,000.
This is to remove a dangerous crossing and build a subway. The cost is estimated at $6,000.
Will the government follow the rule laid down as to the distribution of cost and ask the municipality to pay a share of this amount?
This, will be all paid by the government. The Intercolonial railway pays no taxes to the municipalities as the other railways do.
Having regard to the fact that this railway does not pay taxes, and probably for other reasons, you do not propose to ask the municipalities to contribute anything?
We do not.
Does the Intercolonial pay a frontage sewerage tax to the municipalities as all other land owners do?

My information is that the Intercolonial railway pays no taxes of that kind.
To strengthen bridges, $61,000.
This is for strengthening bridges on the line to accommodate the heavier rolling stock.
Is the whole cost of the strengthening of these bridges charged against capital or against revenue?
The amount charged up to capital would be, less the amount realized on the material in these bridges.

But suppose you have a wooden bridge which has done service up

to the present you could not tear it up and get anything for it. If you are putting in a steel bridge to replace a wooden bridge it seems to me that at least the service cost of the wooden bridge should be contributed from revenue. What is the general principle upon which the strengthening is proceeded with, in other words, what is the total cost of strengthening all the bridges to which you are going to appropriate this money. Is it $61,000 or is it $120,000, the other half being appropriated from current revenue?

This is all being taken out of capital. For instance, if the old rolling stock had remained, very few of these bridges would have needed to be strengthened, unless one of them was worn out entirely, in which case we might have replaced it out of revenue. But where, on account of heavier rolling stock, we have to do away with an old bridge, the bridge becomes useless altogether. It is worth nothing for present use, because heavier rolling stock demands a heavier bridge. It is not like a rail. When you take up a 67-lb. rail you have the rail, but when one of these bridges is removed, it becomes of no value, and I do not see how you could well credit it to anything. It is the common practice of company railways to do that.

I would like to know the principle upon which roads in the United States, under the commission, operate. There must be some statement of the methods of their operation, which the minister could lay on the table of the House for our information.
I will get the principle. If it is not in a concrete form, I will work it out and lay it on the table of the House.

This is an item that appears every year, and I presume will appear for many years to come. May I ask what proportion of the bridges on the Intercolonial have already been strengthened, and how many does he expect to strengthen the coming year?

My information is that the present amount will nearly complete the work this year. If the rolling stock on the line is practically doubled in weight, it will mean that every bridge must be strengthened. There may be two or three bridges in addition to these, but no more. Then if they are renewed afterwards, the cost will come out of revenue.
Chaudiere	Junction-engine house, &c.,

The item has been reduced from $20,000 to $6,000, because we have abandoned the idea of building -a new
engine house. This is to complete the tracks and signals, fire pumps, &c., which are accessories to the round house.
Diversion of line at Chatham, and branch to wharf, $150,000.

This is a large* item. The estimated cost was about $440,000 for building this diversion. I suppose it will be about eight and a half miles. It gets over a heavy grade between Nelson and Loggieville, it shortens the line, and it opens up and gives access to the harbour at Chatham. As a matter of fact, the station is a long way from the harbour, and quite a distance from the town itself.
I visited the place, and was much impressed with the fact that there ought to be some means of getting nearer to the harbour. Everything had to be hauled a long distance. It was represented to me by the Board of Trade, by the council and by a large meeting of citizens, that they had in view some great new industries which they would undertake if they could get the railway nearer deep water. I think, in the interest of the road, that would be one consideration. But there was another thing, and that was getting rid of a very heavy grade and shortening the line. We decided to undertake this work about a year ago. The estimated cost is $440,000, of which we have spent about ' $3,000 on surveys. I have a full estimate of the work in its details. The old road would be abandoned.
What you are really doing is to build the old railway into the city?
To get down into the heart of traffic, and we expect a larger traffic on account of reaching deep water.
Why not take the original route?

The old Canada Eastern did that, but they did not pay much attention to grades. This is bringing the old Canada Eastern railway down into the town of Chatham. At present, it is not on the Intercolonial proper.

This is on a line that we acquired a few years ago, and when this is done will you be right down to the harbour? What is the nature of the work that is going to be done now for this estimated expenditure of $150,000?
We have to get the right of way, grading, ballasting and track laying. We expect to run along the harbour for one or two miles.
Does the $440,000 include anything for harbour improvement, or is it all for railway construction?

It is merely for the railway. I suppose it will include a station. It will necessitate the removal of the station from its present location to a location in the town.
Mr. J1ENNOX. Has the minister at hand a summary of what amount has been spent under the head of capital expenditure on the Canada Eastern railway since we acquired it?

I will get that information for my hon. friend, if possible; it is quite a large amount. There has been ballasting, new bridges and that kind of thing. I think last session I gave the full capital expenditure.
What is the opinion of the minister as to the increase in traffic that you are going to get by adding nearly half a million of expenditure on this branch road?

There seems to be a prospect for a good traffic in lumber and pulp wood. Strong representations were made that a very large mill would probably be erected at that point if they had proper railway facilities.
They have a pulp mill there now.
Yes, they have, I know but it is working under a great disadvantage.
Are they going to build another?

Mv information is that another pulp mill and perhaps a paper mill would be erected there. But, no matter how good the port facilities are the distance that they have to haul of a mile or a mile and a half between the station and the port is an obstacle. If the possibilities are to be developed at all this is the only way in which we can do it. In addition the heavy graue we have there has made it almost impossible to do any business over that line.

The minister is incurring a very large expenditure on very airy grounds. He has no real certainty of anything. Pulp has been remotely considered or suggested. A paper mill may follow. It does not seem to me that we are justified in doubling the amount that we originally paid for the road and which we were told bought a road which was reasonably well constructed and well equipped. We pay out half as much more and there is no certainty at all that the development and extra business which the minister refers to will result. Eailways do not build unless there is some reasonable certainty of securing extra business. We are going to
put into a road that we were told would cost us $800,000 something in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000.

There is a good deal of truth in what my hon. friend says. But in the province of Ontario a great deal of the difficulty that we have had with some of our company railways has been that they have built half a mile or so from the town and if it is possible to give any other railway the business we always do it. It is in the interest of the railway that we should develop the traffic there. You cannot have any guarantee at any of those places. You have to look at the possibility of the trade and overcome one of the charges which have been made against this government road that it will not assist the industries of the maritime provinces as other railways would do. In a port like this it is wise to get to the water front so as to get whatever traffic may be there. In addition we make a great reduction in the grade which has been a handicap in attempting to do any business there.
What service does the Intercolonial railway give to Chatham?
We have a branch line from Chatham Junction, but the station is a mile or a mile and a half away from the the town.
I did not get an answer explicitly from the minister. The minister will furnish us with the total amount which has been expended upon capital account on that eastern railway since we acquired it?
Yes.

I recollect there was a great deal of criticism as to the wisdom of acquiring this railway at the time we did acquire it. It was the Gibson line and it was represented to us that it was in good working condition, would be a very valuable line and that we would not have to expend any considerable sum of money in order to begin immediately to derive a benefit from it. I think it will be found that we have already expended a large sum upon capital, here is an item of $440,000 and we can assume that it will reach half a million or more before it is finished. There is a good deal in the suggestion that there is a very airy possibility of any considerable advantage to be derived from the expenditure on this line. Although I dislike always to speak of the Newmarket canal it is a good deal on the same line as the construction of that expensive work for the purpose of building up one possible industry. It was said that the Kane Bros., would probably leave Newmarket if we did not build that canal and $200,000

or $300,000 was going to do the whole thing. Now we find that it is running into a very large amount of money. I do not want to obstruct the minister in any of these items, but I think we ought to have pretty full information as to what is contemplated as well as what has been done in connection with this Canada Eastern railway.
I will bring all the information down.
Maybe the minister would do just as well to let this item stand and go on with other items, because I think this is rather too important to pass with the information that we have.

If my hon. friend will tell me what he wants I will try to get it. There is no information as to the trade except that a man with practical ideas looks over the ground and comes to the conclusion that there is a possibility of very large development there. The other advantage is that we are getting rid of a grade and bringing down to the sea-board a railway that is a mile or a mile and a half away.
We find $440,000 as one item of proposed expenditure. Is this the total or will we be confronted with other items as we go along?
I do not know but that there may be on this whole length of railway, but this covers everything at Chatham. Anything new that has to be done must be charged to capital account.

Here is a railway that cost us $800,000, and here is one spot on that railway that is to cost more than half a million in addition to what we paid for the railway. What are we to expect in reference to the rest of it? What was suggested by the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was that the minister should let this item stand until we get the information spoken of, and then the minister will probably indicate what other items of capital expenditure are for the construction of this. Of course the minister must know what he contemplates, in addition to this, off-hand.

As I understand the Minister of Railways, this expenditure isjusti-fied on the ground that the branch line will increase in efficiency, whereby its earning power will increase so that you can haul more cheaply.
That is one of the great reasons.

Then how does the minister reconcile this with the line of policy laid down in connection with the Branch
Lines Bill, not to take over any branch lines reported to be not in a good and safe condition? In other words, not to take over a railway that requires expenditure on it.
This railway has been taken over and this is absolutely a new road that we are constructing.

I quite understand that, but the principle is there just the same, you are expending money on a road that has been acquired. I am not speaking in a critical way, because in connection with the Branch Lines Bill I believe that the government should take over a railway even if it is only a rattle-trap road if, after it is placed in proper condition, it will be a paying asset to the government. But I ask if, while you are making an expenditure on this branch line to increase its efficiency, you should not do so in reference to any future road acquired under the Branch Lines Bill?

We are criticised now for taking over a Toad on which we will have to spSnd money, and the Branch Lines Act Tather protects us in the future against that criticism. This road has already been purchased and we want to get the best possible results from it. We want to get down into the town of Chatham, where there is a chance not only of decreasing the grade, but of getting more goods to haul.

Suppose it had been left entirely to this managing board or to the chief engineer just on the ground of the traffic necessities of the road, would they have recommended an expenditure of $400,000 or $500,000 in order to improve the road for the sake of the haulage over it? Is it not a fact that this is another method of paying respect to very strong party jpres-sure which has been made at certain times? This road was acquired in the first place as a result of a political promise. The House was misled, because we were told we were getting a road well worth the money and in a reasonable state of repair and efficiency. I think that from the debates in this House we could show that the minister became sponsor to the House that it would not land us into very much greater expenditures. Here we are increasing the cost price in one little instance by one-half the whole price.

But we are getting a good deal more by the expenditure. This was no political promise, I can assure my hon. friend. If it had been it would have been made to one political party. I visited Chatham and spent some hours there. I met the citizens, I do not know who were Liberals and who were Conservatives. I met the board of trade, the council and citizens generally and I was strongly cen-

sured by the Conservative press there because I did not absolutely promise on the spot that I would do this. I considered it carefully, I had a talk with the chief engineer and the deputy, and while in answer to my hon. friend's question, I think if it were only to improve the haulage for the goods we now have, we would not go to this very large expenditure, it would be worth a large proportion of the expenditure to do that. But, taking into consideration the possibilities of the place, the fact that we are trying to assist the development where we can without too much expense to the railway, feeling that we get a return, I undertook, after full consideration, not as a political promise but as a promise to the citizens and in the interest of transportation and development, to do this work. It is not a political promise in any sense.
What are the freight earnings for Chatham?
I have not those figures with me, there is considerable, freight.

I do not object to having the line put into, the town but it seems a large expenditure, for the exports of Chatham are nearly all lumber and you will not haul lumber over your road, it has to go by water as they have a good harbour and the same thing is true of pulp.
It was not so outlined to us by the prominent business men there. They felt that a great deal of traffic would be developed by the road going to the harbour.
What kind of traffic? They must have told the minister.
It does not follow as a fact that because some hon. gentleman is of opinion that certain traffic will not go by the route, it will not go, because possibly a good deal will be carried.

You must exercise your judgment.
^ Mr. GRAHAM. It is a matter of opinion, that is all. The men of the city were positive that a great deal of traffic would be done on this railway if it got down to the harbour, and a great deal of traffic and merchandise would go to the harbour that does not now go there because the railway is so far off they cannot make connection.

This is a road from Fredericton to Chatham. Wre know the nature of the country through which it runs. It is not a country calculated to throw much traffic into the town of Chatham. What will go to Chatham? The lumber along the streams is taken down the streams to Gibson or Marysville and from there it is shipped on the St. John river. Will this road Mr. GRAHAM.
divert that traffic from that old and cheap route? Most of the lumber must take that route, and will not be shipped on your line even when you add this extra $500,000. Is there much agriculture produce, &c., which will run to the town of Chatham and bring you a return in freightage on that road? That traffic will be very small. What is there in Chatham, now or, to come which will find its outlet by way of Chatham over this Canada Eastern to Fredericton and what is to become of it there?

My hon. friend forgets that this road will work in connection with the Intercolonial railway. It does not necessarily go to Fredericton at all. Traffic goes east and west on the Intercolonial railway. It is a mistake to say that all lumber is shipped by water. A large quantity of the sawn lumber there goes by rail.
W7il] it go by rail from Chatham over this road in the direction of Fredericton?
A large share of it will go to Chatham junction and be shipped on the Intercolonial railway east and west from there.
Over how many miles of road will that accretion go? What will be the haulage you get?

The Intercolonial railway will get all the haulage when it strikes that line. We get it at the junction and by getting to the harbour it is represented we will get a larger trade than we do now. It does not need to go to Fredericton, it goes to the junction and then to St. John by the Intercolonial railway. It is true that we do not get all the haulage on the Canada Eastern branch. While this is a part of the Canada Eastern branch, it will also be a feeder to the Intercolonial railway at the junction point and the Intercolonial railway will take charge of the traffic there.

What has been the net revenue from this Gibson road, say for the last year? That information might enable us to judge how this matter will work out. Is the minister of the opinion that this addition of $440,000 would result in a proportionate net increase of revenue or in a deficit?
My hon. friend must know that this question cannot be answered. In any transportation problem you cannot guarantee that you would get any stated revenue. You look over the ground and hope you will.
What revenue have we been getting in the past from this road?

I answered that question as fully as possible last year, in reply to the hon. member for St. Antoine division,

Montreal. I have not the figures with me at present.
What was the general result-considerable profit?
No, I think not. This year, when the year is up, it may be different.
It would be unfortunate if, with an increase in the expenditure, we had a proportionate increase in the deficit.

I happen to know very well the situation of affairs at Chatham, and I can assure the committee that it would be impossible to project any extension of the railway which is more likely to add to the business of the main line.
In the whole wide world?

Yes, relatively to the business of the main line. As my hon. friend knows, the Miramichi is a very important river, navigable up to Chatham, and even beyond Newcastle. There are important industries there, and the people of Chatham are unanimously of the opinion that this extension along the water front will lead to the establishment of a number of very important industries. They believe that it will give new life to the town, tend to develop large industries and bring to the railroad a great traffic which it could not possibly get unless this connection were made between the water and the railway.

All of which was said by another gentleman, at a different time, and in almost the same words, with reference to the Newmarket canal.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. On the Miramichi there is 20 feet of water.

Well, that is an advantage; there is water there. But there is no plan of this proposed extension; we are entirely in the dark with reference to it. If the minister will gather up some of the information asked for and bring a plan of it when we come to the estimates tomorrow, I think we shall make mpre progress.

I will bring a plan and lay it on the table to-morrow, although I do not think my hon. friend can form much of an idea from an engineer's plan.
Air-brakes to freight cars, $10,000.
How many cars is it expected this will equip?

About 200. We have a total of 12,779 cars, of which we have equipped 10,801, leaving 1,978 tp be equipped. Our cars cannot go across the line if they [DOT]are not equipped with air brakes, even if we did not have them as a measure of .safety.
I suppose the minister intends to have all the freight cars equipped with air brakes?
Yes.
Why does not the minister have the work pushed through? In the different carshops at Moncton, Stel-larton and Halifax, men were laid off. Why were these men not kept at this work?

We are getting along pretty rapidly, having equipped already 10,801 cars.
To exchange drawbars of freight cars, $10,COO.
How many cars will this amount equip?
About 200 cars, which will leave a balance of about 493.
Is this work done in the carshops?
Yes, in our own shops.
What is the reason for exchanging the drawbars?

We have to have a standard drawbar, or no other road will accept our cars. On the old-fashioned car there was a link coupling, which is obsolete and only good for scrap.
General protection of highways - Intercolonial railway, $10,000.
What policy does the minister propose to adopt as regards protection of highways?

This is to place bells for the protection of highways at level cross-ways-either bells or gates. Year by year we are taking a moderate amount and are setting the other railways a good example. We are eliminating some level crossings altogether every year and in other places there will be something for overhead bridges.

I hope the minister will adopt some relative basis as regards protection by gates and bells and overhead crossings and subways. I think the minister will be justified in making to some extent the Intercolonial railway an object lesson to the other railways, especially, in connection with the safety of the public.
Does this include the vote passed last year for the protection of the crossing at Londonderry?
Yes.

It is my duty to brinfe to the minister's attention the bad condition of the roadway and also the station yards at Amherst. Amherst is a town of some 9,000 population. The railway track

divides the town in two. There is a level crossing at Main street, which is guarded in the daytime by an old pensioner, who is away at meal hours and at night time leaves altogether. There is a very large block between the main street and Christie's crossing, about half a mile. On the south side of the highway are a number of factories, employing some 1,600 men, most of whom live on the north side of the track, and their only way to reach their homes is to cross the railway. During the past three or four years, there have been a large number of accidents and several losses of life. Only in December last, a twelve-year-old girl was killed. With the shunting and moving about constantly of the trains the cars are not separated, so that there is no passage way and the result is the children crawl underneath, and in doing so this girl was killed. I would urge that an item be placed in the estimates for the building there of an overhead bridge. In the case of the Chatham branch, we are spending $450,000 to improve the line of railway and the station, and the freight and passenger earnings of that branch only amount to $163,000. In the case of Amherst, the total receipts from freight and passenger earnings, as shown by the Auditor General's Report, amount to $563,000, so that on the basis of dollars and cents, the minister should consider this case. But from the standpoint of human life, there is very great need for an overhead bridge.

An overhead bridge might be built, but as the place is practically level, it would have to be so high that in nine cases out of ten, people would still cross beneath the bridge. At least that is my experience in western towns.

You could build a subway more cheaply, perhaps. Between Christie street crossing and Victoria street crossing, there is a _ street known as Station street. At that point a subway could be continued to opposite the car works and enable the operators to pass back and forth in comparative safety. I know that three or four losses of life have occurred there in the last three or four years. I think a subway could be built there quite cheaply, as there is no rock and the drainage is good. The subway is not only needed for the employees but for their children who live on the south and go to school on the north.
Halifax-increased accommodation, $52,650.

This has been going on for a long while. It is for additional tracks in the yard on the west side of Water street and also for removing buildings in Richmond yard. It is estimated that the pavements will cost $11,500, and the wiring of buildings $5,000.
There was $180,000 voted last year. That will be all spent by the end of the present year too, I presume, and $52,000 more is wanted. Will those- two complete the work?
It would not be honest for me to say that there would not be any more expenditure at a terminal like Halifax, because expenditures will constantly be going on there.
Are all the works included in this $52,000, under contract?

Yes, except the track laying, which is done by ourselves.
Indiantown and Blackville-to put line into condition for operation, $2,000.
What do you mean by putting the line into condition for operation; is it not running now?

There has 'been an expenditure of $168,000 on this Indiantown branch, which includes the building of quite a large 'bridge, and we have it now in practical running order, and this $2,000 will finish the job. It was not in good running order when we got it.
What is the length of the line?
About eight miles.
Will trains be run regularly this year to connect with the trains on the Fredericton and Chatham branch?
I think there is a regular' train connection there now, but I would not. be sure without looking at the time table.

There was some interest in the question as to whether, when the Indiantown branch was open, a traveller from Fredericton to Montreal might go by way of Blackville and Newcastle, instead of by Chatham Junction.
I rather- think the through connection would still be made by Chatham Junction.
Is this the last of this expenditure?

Yes.
Lac au Saumon-overhead crossing, $1,400.
Does this represent the total cost of this bridge?
Yes, the contour of the land there renders it cheap and convenient to erect this bridge.

This is an instance of what I have advocated, that where the formation of the land lent itself to an over-

head bridge like this, a bridge should be erected.
I think so myself.
Thq interest uipon this expenditure is a mere trifle, and it is much better than to employ a watchman.
It is better than a bell and much safer.

It is an illustration of what I have been contending for.
Loggieville-improvements, $12,000.
This is for improvements at the station.
What will be the total cost of these works?
The total estimated cost is $32,000.

Is it the intention to include in the supplementary estimates this year an appropriation for the station at Fredericton? There was an initial vote of $10,000 put in the estimates for 1908, but that vote was dropped from the estimates last year, and it is not included in the main estimates this year. The minister has been to Fredericton and he has recognized the absolute necessity for a new station. The present building is a disgrace to the railway and an eyesore in the community. The board of trade and the city council of Fredericton have taken the matter up, and I would like to hear from the minister if it is the intention to put a vote for a new station at Fredericton in the supplementary estimates?

I would not like to say that. But I agree with my hon. friend that the station at Fredericton is not fit for that city. I may go further, and say that I do not think the station at Truro is fit either. But we are going along gradually. There is some question about our property at Fredericton that has been bothering us considerably, and it is not quite clear yet. I would not like to say that I will put an item in the estimates. But every word my hon. friend says about the station at Fredericton is absolutely true; we must have, before long, a new station at Fredericton.
An initial appropriation was made a year ago. Why was that dropped?

I did not know certain things about the property there that I have found out since, and which it would not be wise perhaps to reveal. But the hon. gentleman will not have to wait long for a station. Last vear I hoped to make some arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway, and join them, but unfortunately we cannot do that.

Can the minister say whether a site has been decided upon? Because I may say that some of the gentlemen who figure prominently in the Liberal organization there are buying up land, and purchases have been made within a week or two by the gentleman who has the patronage of the Liberal party. I would call the attention of the minister to that fact, so that if they have any particular location in view, they may make their purchase of land from the present owners, and not be called upon to pay large profits and rake-offs1 to middlemen.

I think my hon. friend can rest assured that we will guard against that. If we were to give an intimation of where we wished to purchase, I imagine the price would immediately go up. I have not heard the circumstances which my hon. friend has outlined, but he can rest assured that we will buy the land at the lowest possible price, and if we cannot get it at a price which we think reasonable, there is a process by which we can get it at a fair valuation.

Ever since I have been in the House I have advocated a new station at Truro. That station is a disgrace to the road. Amherst has had two new stations since that was built, Pic-tou has had a good station, Stellarton has had one, Antigonish and some other places. I would like the minister to give me some kind of a promise that we will get that station. I feel sure that if the present deputy had remained-I am sorry to see him going-we would have had an item in the estimates for next year.

I know that my present deputy has been studying the question of a station at Truro. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I say something that may sound a little blunt. I think we have designed stations along the Intercolonial, I will not say extravagant but sometimes out of proportion to the needs. My hon. friend has spoken to me about the station at Truro, and we need a new station there. We are studying the question, and it cannot be very long before we shall have to have a new station there, even in our own interest.

I would like to say to the minister in connection with the diversion of the line at Chatham, that if he has not got the information now, I would like him to state, when we return to the item, just what negotiations have taken place with reference to the acquisition of

the right of way, what properties have been purchased, if any, and from whom, and at what prices.
Some resolutions reported.
